Sure thing! Let’s break it down in plain‑English. --- ## 🌟 What is an **internal audit**? An internal audit is a check‑up that **your own team** performs on the virtualQ system. Think of it as a regular health‑check that the engineers, the Head of Engineering, and sometimes the Chief Executive Officer (through the audit board) do themselves. ### How it works | Step | Who’s involved | What happens | |------|----------------|--------------| | **Planning** | Head of Engineering (and sometimes the Chief Executive Officer) | Decide what parts of the system to look at and which “pillars” (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability) to focus on. | | **Execution** | Engineers, architects, and reviewers | • Review code in pull‑request reviews (small decisions).
• Hold dedicated architecture or design meetings for bigger, strategic choices.
• Run internal tools that scan the code base or the live (non‑production) environment. | | **Reporting** | Head of Engineering → whole team | Findings are logged as **technical debt** and ranked by criticality. The team then works on fixing them. | | **Frequency** | Usually **once or twice a year** (but can be more often for specific areas). | ### Why it matters - **You own the process** – you decide what to look at and how quickly to act. - **Fast feedback** – because the same people who build the system are also checking it, issues get spotted early. - **Cost‑effective** – you’re using internal resources and tools you already have. --- ## 🌐 What is an **external audit**? An external audit is a check‑up that **someone outside your organisation** performs. It brings an independent, “fresh‑eyes” perspective. ### Who does it? - **External security advisors** or **partner companies** that specialise in penetration testing and security assessments. - **AWS Well‑Architected Framework** – Amazon offers a self‑service audit tool that evaluates any assets running on AWS (or hybrid) against the same six pillars. ### How it works | Step | Who’s involved | What happens | |------|----------------|--------------| | **Tooling / Service selection** | External vendor (or AWS) | Choose a scanning tool or a penetration‑testing service. | | **Assessment** | Vendor runs automated scans on the **code base** *or* on a **non‑production copy** of the live system. They may also do manual security tests (pen‑tests). | | **Report** | Vendor delivers a formal report with findings, often categorised by severity. | | **Follow‑up** | Your internal team (Head of Engineering, engineers) reviews the report, logs the findings as technical debt, and fixes them. | | **Frequency** | Typically **once or twice a year**, just like internal audits, but can be scheduled after major releases or when compliance demands it. | ### Why it matters - **Objectivity** – an outsider isn’t influenced by internal shortcuts or assumptions. - **Specialist expertise** – external partners often have deep security knowledge and tools you might not own. - **Compliance** – many regulations (e.g., NIS2) require proof that an independent party has looked at your security posture. --- ## 🔄 Key Differences at a Glance | Aspect | Internal Audit | External Audit | |--------|----------------|----------------| | **Who conducts it?** | Your own engineers, Head of Engineering, internal reviewers | Independent security advisors, partner firms, or cloud‑provider tools (e.g., AWS Well‑Architected) | | **Perspective** | “Inside‑looking” – knows the day‑to‑day quirks | “Outside‑looking” – unbiased, fresh view | | **Tools** | Internal tooling, code reviews, pull‑request checks | External tooling/services, manual pen‑tests, AWS audit console | | **Scope** | Often broader (operational, cost, sustainability) and tied to internal processes | Usually focused on security and compliance, but can also cover the six pillars via AWS | | **Frequency** | Usually once/twice a year, but can be ad‑hoc | Usually once/twice a year, often aligned with compliance calendars | | **Outcome** | Findings become internal technical debt; decisions made in internal meetings | Formal report handed over; may be required for regulatory proof | | **Cost** | Mostly internal staff time (lower direct cost) | Vendor fees, tool licences (higher direct cost) | --- ## 🎯 Bottom line - **Internal audits** are your team’s own health‑check. They’re great for day‑to‑day improvements, quick feedback, and keeping the whole crew aligned on best practices. - **External audits** bring an independent, expert eye that can catch things your team might miss and provide the compliance evidence regulators (like NIS2) often demand. Both are important, and they complement each other nicely: internal audits keep the ship sailing smoothly, while external audits make sure the hull is watertight. 🚢💪 Hope that clears things up! If you want to dive deeper into any specific pillar or need tips on setting up the next audit, just let me know.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Sure thing! VirtualQ bundles two “smart” optimization engines into its platform, and each one is built for a slightly different purpose. Here’s a quick rundown of the two optimizers and what they actually do:

| Optimizer | What it’s called | What it does (in plain‑English) |
|-----------|------------------|---------------------------------|
| **Automated Flexible Optimizer** | **AFO** | Think of AFO as a very adaptable rule‑engine. It looks at the data you feed it (like staffing levels, service‑level targets, cost limits, etc.) and then automatically tweaks the schedule or resource allocation to meet those constraints. Because it’s “flexible,” you can change the business rules on the fly—add a new priority, tighten a budget, or relax a timing rule—and the optimizer will re‑run without needing a full redesign. |
| **Automated Predictive Optimizer** | **APO** | APO goes a step further by using machine‑learning models to *predict* what will happen next (e.g., call‑volume spikes, ticket‑arrival patterns, demand surges) and then optimizes based on those forecasts. It learns from historical training data, continuously improves its predictions, and then automatically creates the best‑possible plan (staffing, routing, capacity, etc.) that balances cost, service quality, and compliance. |

### How they fit together

1. **AFO** is great when you have a solid set of known constraints and you need a quick, reliable way to keep everything in balance. It’s the “plug‑and‑play” optimizer that can be re‑configured without a data‑science team.

2. **APO** shines when the environment is more dynamic and you want the system to *anticipate* changes before they happen. By training on past data (the “Training Data” section of the docs) it can forecast demand and proactively adjust resources.

Both optimizers live inside VirtualQ’s AI/ML layer (see the “Further Use of AI/ML in the virtualQ System” heading) and are continuously improved through automated code reviews and external audits. In practice, a company might start with AFO to get immediate value, then layer APO on top as they collect more data and want predictive, self‑learning optimization.

Hope that clears things up! Let me know if you’d like a deeper dive into how the training data feeds the APO, or how you can toggle between the two in the VirtualQ console.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

response:
Great question! 😊

When it comes to using third-party software or services at virtualQ, we need to make sure everything is not only effective but also legally safe — especially since we handle sensitive data protected by strict rules like the **EU’s GDPR** and other high-level regulations (like for KRITIS or social code/SGB customers).

So, the **legal criteria** for any third-party software include:

1. **Data Privacy & Location**:  
   We carefully check where the service stores and processes data. Since our customers’ data is highly sensitive, we must ensure it stays within legal boundaries (e.g., in GDPR-compliant regions). If a third-party service could *potentially* access our data, even in theory, we need to be extra cautious.

2. **Data Processing Agreements (DPAs)**:  
   Any third-party service that handles personal data on our behalf may need to be listed in our DPAs with clients. This means the service must support GDPR-compliant processing and sign appropriate agreements with us.

3. **Licenses & Intellectual Property (IP)**:  
   For open-source tools or commercial libraries, we review the license to make sure:
   - It’s safe to use in a **commercial product**.
   - We won’t run into problems if we want to **sell or transfer** the virtualQ system later (like in an exit scenario).
   - The license doesn’t impose unwanted restrictions (like forcing us to open-source our own code).

In short: before we adopt any third-party tool, we double-check that it’s **legally safe**, **privacy-compliant**, and won’t put us (or our customers) at risk now or down the road. 🛡️✅

Let me know if you'd like examples of tools we’ve evaluated!
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

We use a few different programming languages, each chosen for a specific purpose to make the system work well and stay easy to maintain.

Right now, the main languages we use are:

- **Ruby and Elixir** – These handle the core application logic. They’re reliable and great for building scalable, long-lasting systems.

response:
Great question! Let me break it down in a simple way.

**Internal audits** are checks that your own team does to make sure everything is built and running the right way. At virtualQ, these happen regularly and involve things like:

- Team discussions about system design and architecture
- Code reviews (where engineers check each other’s work before it goes live)
- Using tools like the **AWS Well-Architected Framework** to review cloud systems — this looks at things like security, reliability, and performance
- Tracking any issues found as "technical debt" so they can be fixed later based on how important they are

These internal checks help catch problems early and keep the system strong and secure.

On the other hand, **external audits** are done by people or tools *outside* your company. For virtualQ, this includes:

- Using third-party tools or services to scan the code or test the system in a safe, non-production environment
- Hiring expert security partners to do **penetration testing** — basically, they try to hack the system (in a good way!) to find weak spots before bad guys do

So, the main difference is:
- **Internal audits** = your own team reviewing and improving the system
- **External audits** = outside experts or tools giving an objective check for security and quality

Both are super important — they work together like double-checking your work with a teammate and then having a teacher review it too!
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

response:
Great question! 😊

virtualQ offers two main optimizers: the **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** and the **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)**.

Here’s what they do in simple terms:

- The **AFO (Automated Flexible Optimizer)** helps make the system more adaptable and efficient by automatically adjusting settings based on current needs. Think of it like a smart thermostat that tweaks things in real time to keep everything running smoothly.

- The **APO (Automated Predictive Optimizer)** takes it a step further by using patterns and data to *predict* what the system will need in the future. It proactively makes adjustments to prevent issues before they happen—kind of like how weather forecasts help you decide whether to carry an umbrella.

Together, these optimizers help virtualQ stay fast, reliable, and smart—especially important when working with enterprise clients who need high performance and uptime.

And if you're curious, virtualQ uses training data to help power these AI-driven features, making them even smarter over time! 🚀
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

Hi there! I see you're interested in the legal criteria for using 3rd party software. Let's break it down together in simple terms.

First off, since we handle data that’s regulated by rules like the EU’s GDPR, we have to be very careful about data privacy. This means that any software or service we use from third-party providers must meet strict privacy standards.

Here are the main points we consider:

1. **Legal Compliance (GDPR):** We need to make sure that the 3rd party software complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This is really important because GDPR sets high standards for protecting personal data.

2. **Data Privacy Agreements:** We carefully review data privacy agreements to make sure that the software provider respects our clients' privacy and handles data properly. If the provider is based in a different location, they need to be listed in the Data Protection Agreements (DPAs).

3. **Licenses and Intellectual Property (IP):** We also look at the licenses to understand what we can and cannot do with the software. This includes making sure the software can be integrated into our system without any legal hiccups.

4. **Operational Risk:** We want to avoid situations where we might be stuck with a software that becomes obsolete or isn't supported anymore (this is known as "lock-in").

5. **Security Testing:** Tools like Snyk and Dependabot help us test for vulnerabilities and missing security patches in the software we use. This ensures that the software is secure and reliable.

In summary, the legal criteria ensure that we use 3rd party software that is compliant with regulations, respects data privacy, and won't cause any legal or operational issues in the future. Does that make sense? Feel free to ask if you need more details or have other questions!

Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

Absolutely, let's break this down in a friendly, easy-to-understand way!

### Internal Audits:

Think of internal audits as a kind of quality check that happens within your team. Here’s how it works:
- **What It Is:** Internal audits are like mini-investigations done by people within the company to look at the system and its design.
- **Who Does It:** Usually, engineers and possibly the Head of Engineering get involved.
- **How It Happens:** They might review the code, have special sessions to discuss the system architecture and design, or hold meetings to talk about best practices and potential issues.
- **Frequency:** These could happen as often as needed, but typically once or twice a year.
- **Focus:** They ensure that the system follows best practices and helps spot any areas that need improvement (like technical debt).

### External Audits:

Now, external audits are a bit different—they are like inviting a professional to check your system for you:
- **What It Is:** External audits are done by third-party partners who specialize in security and system checks.
- **Who Does It:** These are carried out by external security advisors or specialized firms.
- **How It Happens:** They might use special tools to check either the code directly or the live system in a non-production environment. It can also include manual security audits like penetration testing.
- **Frequency:** This could also happen once or twice a year, depending on the needs.
- **Focus:** They ensure compliance with external standards and bring an outside perspective that internal teams might miss.

### How They Differ:

- **Source:** Internal audits are done by people within your company, while external audits are performed by outside specialists.
- **Scope:** Internal audits focus on design, architecture, and internal best practices. External audits focus on security, compliance, and might give a broader view of potential vulnerabilities.

Hope this clears up the difference between internal and external audits! If you have more questions, feel free to ask!
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

response:
Great question! VirtualQ offers two different optimizers to help improve their systems and processes: the **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** and the **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)**.

The **AFO** is designed to give flexibility in how it optimizes your systems. It can adapt to various scenarios and make adjustments on the fly to keep things running smoothly.

The **APO**, on the other hand, uses predictive analytics. This means it can anticipate potential issues and make preemptive adjustments to prevent problems before they happen. 

Both of these optimizers are part of virtualQ's commitment to continually improving and providing the best possible service to their clients. They work together to ensure that everything is running as efficiently and securely as possible.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

response:
Sure thing! When you’re thinking about bringing a 3rd‑party library or service into a product like **virtualQ**, there are a handful of legal “check‑points” you want to run through. Here’s a quick, friendly rundown of the main criteria:

| **What to look at** | **Why it matters** | **What you should do** |
|---------------------|--------------------|------------------------|
| **GDPR compliance** | The data you handle is subject to the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation. If the 3rd‑party tool processes or stores personal data, it must meet GDPR’s strict rules (lawful basis, data‑subject rights, breach notification, etc.). | Verify the vendor’s privacy policy, data‑processing agreement (DPA) and any GDPR‑specific certifications. Make sure you can sign a DPA that lists the vendor as a processor. |
| **Geolocation / data residency** | Some regulations (and even your own contracts) require that data stay within certain countries or regions. | Ask where the vendor’s servers are located and whether they can guarantee data stays in an approved region (e.g., EU‑only). |
| **Data‑privacy agreements** | Even if the vendor is GDPR‑compliant, you still need a clear contract that spells out who can see the data, how it’s protected, and what happens on termination. | Include a DPA, confidentiality clauses, and clear “data‑access” provisions in your contract. |
| **Listing in your own DPA** | virtualQ’s customers may need to see every downstream processor listed in the DPA you share with them. | Ensure the vendor agrees to be listed (or that you can document the relationship) so you stay transparent with your clients. |
| **License type & compatibility** | Open‑source components come with a variety of licenses (MIT, Apache, GPL, etc.). Some are “viral” (e.g., GPL) and can force you to open‑source your own code, which may not be acceptable for a commercial product. | Identify the exact license, check whether it allows commercial use, redistribution, and whether it conflicts with other licenses you already use. |
| **IP ownership** | You need to know who owns the code you’re pulling in and whether you have the right to modify, redistribute, or sell it. | Get a written statement (often part of the license or a separate agreement) confirming you have the necessary rights. |
| **“Appropriate” for commercial/exist‑scenario** | The term “appropriate” in the internal policy means the component can be used in a product you sell or that you can hand over to a buyer if you ever exit the business. | Confirm the license permits commercial exploitation and that there are no hidden clauses that would block a future sale or transfer. |
| **Sector‑specific rules** | If your customers are under special regulations (e.g., Germany’s Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB) or KRITIS for critical infrastructure), the bar is even higher than plain GDPR. | Double‑check that the vendor’s security and privacy controls meet those extra requirements (often documented in security certifications or audit reports). |
| **Operational risk tie‑in** | Legal compliance is part of the broader risk picture – you don’t want a legal snag to become an operational nightmare later. | Treat the legal review as a step in the overall risk assessment (together with security scans like Snyk or Dependabot). |

### TL;DR (the short version)

1. **GDPR & privacy** – make sure the vendor can sign a DPA and keep data where you need it.  
2. **Licensing** – know exactly which open‑source license applies and whether it allows commercial use, redistribution, and future sale.  
3. **IP ownership** – confirm you have the rights to use, modify, and ship the code.  
4. **Sector‑specific rules** – for customers under SGB, KRITIS, etc., the vendor must meet those stricter standards.  
5. **Transparency** – the vendor should be listable in your own DPA so your clients know who’s handling their data.

If you tick all those boxes, you’ll be in a solid legal position to use the 3rd‑party software without running into surprises later on. 😊

• Pull‑request reviews
• Internal “audit” meetings | • Operational Excellence
• Security
• Reliability
• Performance Efficiency

• Each finding is ranked by criticality and tracked until it’s fixed | • Looks at the **code base**, data‑flow diagrams, deployment pipelines, etc.

• Verification that the system meets external regulations (e.g., NIS2, GDPR) | Usually **once or twice a year**, but can be triggered by a major release or regulatory requirement | | **What you’ll see** | • A report from the external partner or tool
• Findings are often labeled as “findings” or “issues” rather than “technical debt”
• Recommendations may include remediation steps, policy updates, or evidence of compliance | • Checks that **you** can’t easily do yourself because they need an unbiased view or special tools (e.g., cloud‑service self‑service audit, third‑party pen‑test). | ### Why bring in outsiders? - **Objectivity** – an external team isn’t biased by internal shortcuts or “we’ve always done it this way.” - **Specialised expertise** – penetration testers, compliance specialists, and cloud‑audit services have tools and knowledge that most internal teams don’t. - **Regulatory proof** – many standards (like NIS2) require an independent audit to demonstrate compliance. --- ## The key differences in a nutshell | Aspect | Internal audit | External audit | |--------|----------------|----------------| | **Who performs it** | Your own engineers, architects, and leadership | Independent consultants, security partners, or automated third‑party services | | **Main goal** | Continuous improvement and tracking of technical debt | Validation of security/compliance and unbiased verification | | **Scope** | Deep dive into day‑to‑day implementation, design decisions, and internal processes | Broad check of architecture, security posture, and compliance against external standards | | **Tools** | Pull‑request reviews, internal checklists, design workshops | Automated cloud‑audit tools (e.g., AWS Well‑Architected), external pen‑testing suites, consultancy reports | | **Frequency** | Usually 1–2 times a year, plus ad‑hoc reviews | Usually 1–2 times a year, often aligned with regulatory cycles | | **Outcome format** | Technical‑debt tickets, internal action items | Formal audit report, compliance evidence, remediation recommendations | --- ### TL;DR - **Internal audits** are “in‑house” health‑checks run by the people who build and run the system. They help you stay aligned with your own best‑practice pillars and turn gaps into manageable technical debt. - **External audits** are “outside‑the‑fence” examinations by independent experts or automated services. They give you an unbiased view, prove you meet regulatory requirements (like NIS2), and often uncover security issues you might miss internally. Both types are important: internal audits keep the day‑to‑day ship sailing smoothly, while external audits make sure the ship meets safety regulations and can survive a storm. 🚢✨
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

response:
Sure thing! VirtualQ bundles two “smart‑engine” tools that automatically keep the platform humming along as your workload changes. They’re called **optimizers**, and each one focuses on a slightly different job:

| Optimizer | What it does (in plain language) |
|-----------|-----------------------------------|
| **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** | Think of AFO as the “real‑time‑adjuster.” It watches what’s happening in the system right now—how many users are logged in, what kind of requests are coming in, how much CPU or memory is being used—and then instantly tweaks things (adds or removes resources, re‑balances traffic, etc.) so the app stays fast and stable. Because it’s “flexible,” you can set policies (e.g., “never let response time go above X ms”) and AFO will keep the system within those bounds. |
| **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** | APO is the “forecast‑planner.” It digs into the historical data that VirtualQ has collected (think past traffic spikes, seasonal usage patterns, typical job‑run times) and uses machine‑learning models to **predict** what the load will look like in the near future. With that insight, it can pre‑emptively spin up capacity, schedule maintenance, or re‑allocate resources so you avoid bottlenecks before they even appear. In short, it helps you stay ahead of demand rather than just reacting to it. |

### How they fit together
- **AFO** is great for handling the day‑to‑day ebb and flow—quick, on‑the‑fly adjustments.
- **APO** adds a longer‑term, data‑driven layer, giving you a heads‑up so the system can be prepared in advance.

Both optimizers are part of VirtualQ’s broader AI/ML toolkit (the same “Training Data” and “Further Use of AI/ML” sections you saw in the doc). By combining real‑time flexibility with predictive foresight, VirtualQ can keep enterprise‑grade applications scalable, secure, and cost‑efficient—exactly the kind of reliability that regulated industries need. 

Hope that clears things up! If you’d like a deeper dive into how each optimizer is configured or what kind of metrics they monitor, just let me know. 😊
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

- Ensuring compliance with data privacy regulations, particularly the EU’s GDPR, as the data handled is subject to strict privacy requirements.
- Carefully considering the geo-location of services and data privacy agreements, especially for services provided by third-party providers, as they may need to be listed in the Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
- Evaluating licenses and intellectual property (IP) ownership, particularly when integrating open-source components into the virtualQ system.
- Ensuring that the licenses allow for commercial use and can be sold along with the virtualQ system in an exit scenario (i.e., "appropriate" licensing).
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits are reviews conducted within the organization, typically involving team members such as the Head of Engineering, and focus on architecture, design, and implementation decisions. These audits may include the use of the AWS Well-Architected Framework, which is a self-service audit assessing cloud or hybrid infrastructure across six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability. The findings from these audits are reviewed internally, tracked as technical debt, and followed up based on criticality. Internal audits also include verification through pull request reviews for smaller decisions and dedicated internal meetings for larger architectural or strategic decisions.

External audits involve the use of external tooling or services to verify the virtualQ system, either at the code base level or on the live system in a non-production environment. Additionally, manual security-related audits such as penetration testing are carried out by an external partner. These audits provide an outside perspective on the system’s security and compliance.

The main difference lies in the origin and scope: internal audits are organization-led, focusing on design, architecture, and operational best practices using internal expertise and frameworks, while external audits rely on third-party tools and experts to validate system security and integrity independently.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

1. **Data Privacy and GDPR Compliance**: Given that the data involved is regulated by the EU’s GDPR, any 3rd party software must have data privacy agreements that are carefully considered. Services run by 3rd party providers might need to be listed in the Data Protection Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
   
2. **Licenses and IP Ownership**: Licenses are crucial for integrating open source components into the virtualQ system. It is important to evaluate licenses to ensure they are appropriate for commercial use or for an exit scenario.

3. **Evaluation of Compliance**: GDPR, customers regulated under the social code (Sozialgesetzbuch, SGB), and customers running critical infrastructure (KRITIS) have specific requirements beyond those defined by the Federal Office of IT Security (BSI).
   
4. **Operational Risk**: Any 3rd party software must ensure that it does not lead to legal issues, does not result in a dead end (such as lock-in or End of Life (EoL) scenarios), and provides proven value.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits are conducted by engineers and verified during pull request reviews for smaller decisions. Larger (strategic) decisions or architectural guardrails are created in dedicated internal meetings or audits. These internal audits include architecture and design sessions within the team.

External audits are based on external tooling/services verifying the virtualQ system, either in the code base or the live system in a non-production stage. Additionally, manual security-related audits (penetration testing) are carried out by a partner. These audits focus on six different pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability) and show where an implementation diverges from best practices. External audits are carried out once or twice a year, and findings are tracked as technical debt and followed up on according to their criticality.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

**Legal criteria for using 3rd‑party software (as defined in the document)**  

1. **Data‑protection & privacy compliance**  
   * The software must respect EU‑GDPR requirements.  
   * Its hosting location (geo‑location) and the associated data‑privacy agreements have to be reviewed, because the service may need to be listed in the Data‑Processing Agreements (DPAs) that *virtualQ* shares with its clients.

2. **Regulatory fit for special‑customer groups**  
   * If the software will be used for customers subject to the German Social Code (SGB) or for operators of critical infrastructure (KRITIS), it must meet the stricter obligations that go beyond the baseline set by the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI).

3. **License and IP ownership**  
   * The software’s licence must be examined to ensure that it allows integration into the *virtualQ* system, commercial use, and possible resale in an exit scenario.  
   * Open‑source components must have licences that are compatible with the required privacy level and that do not give any third party (even in theory) unwanted access to the data.

4. **“Appropriate” use**  
   * A licence is deemed “appropriate” only when the component can be used in a commercial setting and can be sold together with the *virtualQ* product, if needed.

In short, the legal assessment looks at GDPR and other data‑privacy obligations, service geo‑location, DPA inclusion, compliance with sector‑specific regulations (SGB, KRITIS, BSI), and the suitability of the software’s licence and IP rights for commercial integration and future exit scenarios.

Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
**Internal audits**  
- Carried out by the virtualQ team itself (Head of Engineering, engineers, internal architecture‑ and design‑sessions).  
- Include internal reviews of the code base, pull‑request checks, and internal meetings that set strategic or architectural guardrails.  
- Follow the same six‑pillar framework used for all audits — Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability.  
- Findings are recorded as technical debt and are tracked and remediated according to their criticality.  
- Typically performed once or twice a year as part of the regular audit schedule.

**External audits**  
- Performed with external tooling or services that inspect the virtualQ system either in the code repository or in a live, non‑production environment.  
- Additional manual security audits (e.g., penetration testing) are executed by a partner or an external security advisor.  
- May also use third‑party frameworks such as the AWS Well‑Architected Framework, which provides a self‑service audit for cloud or hybrid assets.  
- Like internal audits, they evaluate the same six pillars and report deviations from best‑practice.

**Key differences**  

| Aspect | Internal audit | External audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Who conducts it** | Internal staff (engineers, Head of Engineering, internal reviewers) | Third‑party tools, external partners, security advisors |
| **Method** | Pull‑request reviews, internal architecture/design sessions, internal meetings | Automated scans of code/live system, manual penetration testing, external frameworks (e.g., AWS Well‑Architected) |
| **Scope of review** | Day‑to‑day code quality, strategic/architectural decisions, internal technical debt | Compliance verification, security hardening, validation of the system against external best‑practice standards |
| **Perspective** | Internal view of the product and processes | Independent, outsider view that can uncover issues not seen internally |
| **Output** | Findings logged as technical debt for internal follow‑up | Findings reported by the external party, often with recommendations and formal compliance evidence |

Both audit types use the same six‑pillar evaluation model and are scheduled one to two times per year, but they differ in who performs the review, the tools used, and the perspective they bring to the assessment.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

response:
Internal audits involve reviews conducted within the organization, focusing on areas such as architecture and design through team sessions, pull request reviews, and dedicated internal meetings. Smaller technical decisions are typically made and verified by engineers during development, while larger strategic or architectural decisions are addressed in formal internal audits or meetings. One example is the use of the AWS Well-Architected Framework, a self-service audit assessing cloud or hybrid infrastructure across six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability. This audit is conducted once or twice a year, with findings tracked as technical debt and addressed based on criticality. Participants include the Head of Engineering.

External audits rely on external tooling or services to evaluate the virtualQ system, either in the code base or in a non-production environment. They also include manual security assessments such as penetration testing carried out by a partner. Participants in these audits include the Chief Executive Officer, Head of Engineering, and an external security advisor.

The key difference lies in the scope and conduct: internal audits focus on design verification and operational practices using internal resources and frameworks, while external audits involve third-party tools and experts to validate security and system integrity independently.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Demo
Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden: 
a) Termine für die Service Line im Dashboard aktivieren (nur als Admin möglich)b) Öffnungszeiten sowie Terminliche Rahmenbedingungen konfigurierenc) Einen Callflow auswählen, der “appointment” enthält.
Warum ein neuer Voice Bot? (Nutzen)
Der neue Bot bietet den Vorteil, dass der Kunde selbst entscheiden kann ob er/sie den nächstmöglichen Termin  (also wie ganz normales Queuing) oder einenspäteren Termin bucht. Für den Endkunden bietet das somit eine bessere User Experience. Eine bessere user Experience wird außerdem geschaffen in dem derKunde nicht mehr einer Liste von Terminen anhören muss um diese dann ggf. mit den Tasten zu bestätigen. Der Kunde kann ganz einfach und intuitiv durch Spracheeinen Termin buchen. Dies steigert außerdem die Akzeptanz von Bots.

The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

1. **Compliance with GDPR**: Any data privacy agreements are carefully considered, especially for services run by 3rd party service providers, as they might have to be listed in the Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.

2. **Licenses and IP Ownership**: Licenses are evaluated to ensure they are suitable for integrating open source components into the virtualQ system. This is crucial for maintaining high requirements in the field of privacy.

3. **Appropriate Use**: Licenses should be “appropriate” for use in a commercial setting and should allow for sale along with the virtualQ system in an exit scenario.

4. **Regulatory Requirements**: Special considerations are given for customers regulated under GDPR, the social code (Sozialgesetzbuch, SGB), and those who run critical infrastructure (KRITIS) as they have requirements beyond what is defined by the Federal Office of IT Security (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik, BSI).
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits are carried out once or twice a year and focus on six different pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability. Findings from internal audits are tracked as technical debt and followed up on according to their criticality. Internal audits include activities such as internal and external reviews, architecture and design sessions in the team, and dedicated internal meetings for larger (strategic) decisions or architectural guardrails.

External audits are also based on external tooling/services that verify the virtualQ system - either in the code base or the live system in a non-production stage. Further manual security-related audits, such as penetration testing, are carried out by a partner.

The key difference is that internal audits are performed by the team within the organization, while external audits involve external tooling/services and partners.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Beschreibung
Durch den Appointment2.0 Bot ist es möglich Termine direkt am Telefon zu buchen. Der Unterschied zum alten Termine per Voice ist, dass nicht mehr 3 Terminevom Bot vorgeschlagen werden und der Kunde diese durch drücken von Tasten bestätigen kann, sondern der Kunde kann selbst einen für ihn/ihr passendenTermin vorschlagen. Durch Speech Recognition (Spracherkennung) erkennt der Bot die “Eingabe“ des Kunden und kann darauf reagieren. Das drücken von Tastenist nicht mehr nötig. Alles passiert über Sprache. 
Ist der Appointment Bot aktiviert wird der Anrufer sofort zum Appointment Bot weitergeleitet. Dem Kunden wird dann vom Bot der frühstmögliche Termin angeboten(wie beim Queueing). Der Kunde kann diesen frühst möglichen Termin, dann per DTMF “1” akzeptieren oder mit “2” ablehnen und dann per Sprache einen anderenTermin buchen. Entschließt sich der Kunde einen anderen Termin zu buchen, dann nennt der Bot den Zeitraum in dem Termine zur Verfügung stehen (je nachdemwie es im Dashboard konfiguriert wurde), z.B. “Wir bieten Termine im Zeitraum von Montag bis Freitag den 26.04 von 10 bis 18 Uhr an“. Der Kunde kann nun seinenTermin buchen. 
Einrichtung
Um den Appointment Bot per Voice zu aktivieren muss die folgende Schritte ausgeführt werden:

**Legal criteria for using 3rd‑party software (as defined in the document)**  

1. **Data‑protection compliance**  
   * The software must respect the EU’s GDPR requirements.  
   * Its data‑processing location (geo‑location) and associated privacy agreements have to be examined and approved.

2. **Data‑processing agreements (DPAs)**  
   * If the 3rd‑party service processes data on behalf of virtualQ, it may need to be listed in the DPAs that virtualQ shares with its clients.

3. **Licensing and IP ownership**  
   * The license of the component must be compatible with commercial use and with the virtualQ product‑exit scenario (“appropriate” use).  
   * IP ownership must be clear, especially when integrating open‑source components.

4. **Sector‑specific regulatory requirements**  
   * For customers subject to the German Social Code (SGB) or operating critical infrastructure (KRITIS), the software must meet the stricter obligations defined by those regulations.  
   * It must also satisfy any additional rules set by the Federal Office of IT Security (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik).

5. **Risk of data exposure**  
   * Any party that could, even theoretically, gain access to virtualQ’s data must be evaluated, ensuring that privacy‑risk is acceptable.

In short, the legal assessment checks GDPR and privacy compliance, service geo‑location, DPA inclusion, license suitability and IP clarity, and conformity with higher‑level regulations (SGB, KRITIS, Federal IT‑Security Office) to avoid legal or lock‑in problems.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
**Internal Audits**

* **Who conducts them:** The internal audit is carried out by the *Head of Engineering* and the engineering team itself. Smaller decisions are made by individual engineers and verified in pull‑request reviews; larger, strategic or architectural decisions are discussed in dedicated internal meetings or audits.  
* **What they cover:** Internal and external (i.e., cross‑team) reviews of the architecture and design, as well as regular *internal design‑verification sessions* within the team.  
* **Scope & focus:** The audit checks the implementation against the six pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability) and records any divergences as *technical debt* to be followed up according to criticality.  
* **Frequency:** Typically performed *once or twice a year* and the findings are tracked internally.

**External Audits**

* **Who conducts them:** External audits rely on *third‑party tooling/services* or *partner organizations*.  For security‑related checks a partner performs manual penetration testing, and the *AWS Well‑Architected Framework* provides a self‑service audit for cloud or hybrid assets.  
* **What they cover:** Verification of the virtualQ system – either in the code base or the live system (in a non‑production stage) – using external tools, plus dedicated security penetration tests.  
* **Scope & focus:** The same six pillars are examined, but the assessment is performed from an outside perspective, checking that the implementation conforms to industry‑wide best practices and compliance requirements.  
* **Frequency:** Also performed *once or twice a year*, with findings recorded as technical debt and prioritized by criticality.

**Key Differences**

| Aspect | Internal Audit | External Audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Conducted by** | Head of Engineering & internal engineers | Third‑party tooling, external security partner, AWS Well‑Architected service |
| **Primary activities** | Pull‑request reviews, internal architecture/design sessions, internal meetings | Automated scans of code/live system, manual penetration testing, AWS self‑service review |
| **Perspective** | Internal view, focuses on day‑to‑day engineering decisions | Independent, external view that validates against broader best‑practice and compliance standards |
| **Tooling** | Internal review processes, PR checks | External tooling/services, partner‑performed security tests |
| **Outcome handling** | Tracked as technical debt within the team | Tracked similarly as technical debt but validated by an external source |

In short, **internal audits** are performed by the organization’s own engineering leadership and staff to ensure day‑to‑day compliance with the six pillars, while **external audits** bring in independent tools and partners to independently verify the system’s security and architectural soundness, often providing an additional layer of assurance and compliance verification.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.
