Sure thing! When you’re looking at a 3rd‑party library, tool or service, the “legal” side is all about making sure you can use it safely, without breaking any laws or contracts, and that you keep your customers’ data protected. Here’s a quick, plain‑English checklist of the main legal criteria we usually run through at virtualQ: | ✅ What to check | Why it matters | |-----------------|----------------| | **1. GDPR & EU data‑privacy compliance** | We handle personal data that falls under the EU General Data Protection Regulation. The vendor must respect GDPR rules (e.g., lawful basis for processing, data‑subject rights, breach‑notification obligations). | | **2. Data‑processing agreements (DPAs)** | If the 3rd‑party will touch any of our data, the service has to be listed in the DPAs we already share with our clients. This shows we have a formal contract that spells out each party’s responsibilities. | | **3. Geo‑location of the service** | The physical location of the servers matters because different countries have different privacy rules. We need to know where the data lives and be sure the location is allowed under GDPR (or any sector‑specific rules like SGB or KRITIS). | | **4. License type & IP ownership** | • The licence must explicitly allow **commercial use and resale** of the whole product.
• It must be compatible with any other open‑source components we use.
• We must be sure we own—or have a clear right to use—the IP we’re incorporating, so we don’t get sued later. | | **5. Ability to apply security patches** | Even though this feels more “technical,” it’s a legal requirement under GDPR’s “security of processing” principle. The vendor must provide timely updates and let us apply them without restriction. | | **6. No lock‑in or end‑of‑life (EoL) surprises** | We need to be sure the component won’t disappear tomorrow (or become unsupported) because that could force us into a breach of contract with our customers. | | **7. Documentation & maintainability** | The software should be well documented so that **someone other than the original author** can maintain it. This reduces the risk of a “single‑point‑of‑failure” that could later become a legal liability. | | **8. Certifications that back up the security claims** (often listed under “legal” because they’re required by contracts) | ISO 27001/27017/27018, BSI C5, FIPS 140‑2/3, etc. These certifications demonstrate that the provider follows recognised security standards, which many of our customers (especially those under SGB or KRITIS) demand in their contracts. | ### Putting it all together When we evaluate a third‑party product we basically ask: 1. **Can we use it commercially and sell our solution with it inside?** (License/IP check) 2. **Does the vendor respect GDPR and any extra privacy rules that our customers need?** (Data‑privacy & DPA check) 3. **Is the service hosted in an acceptable location and does it have the right certifications?** (Geo‑location & security standards) 4. **Will we be able to keep it secure and maintain it over time?** (Patch policy, documentation, lock‑in risk) If the answer to all of those is “yes,” the software passes our legal‑criteria gate and we can move forward with confidence. Hope that clears things up! Let me know if you want to dive deeper into any particular point. 😊
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

The system you’re looking at (VirtualQ) builds its core on **two main frameworks**:

1. **Ruby on Rails** – a “Model‑View‑Controller” (MVC) framework written in Ruby. It handles the server‑side logic: receiving data from users or APIs, processing it, and storing it in the database.

2. **React + Redux** – a pair of front‑end frameworks.  
   * **React** lets developers create the user interface as reusable components.  
   * **Redux** works alongside React to keep the app’s state (the data that drives the UI) organized and predictable.

Together, Ruby on Rails powers the back‑end and React/Redux powers the front‑end, giving you a full‑stack foundation for the application.

**Let’s break it down in plain English.** An **audit** is just a systematic check‑up to see whether a system (in this case the virtualQ platform) is built and run the right way. Think of it like a health‑check‑up for software and infrastructure. --- ## 1. Internal audits | What they are | Who does them | How they’re done | When they happen | What they look at | |---------------|--------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------| | A review carried out **inside the company** by the people who own the product. | Mostly the **Head of Engineering**, the engineering team, and sometimes the Chief Executive Officer or a security officer. | • Automated checks using the team’s own tools (e.g., AWS Well‑Architected self‑service checks).
• Manual spot‑checks during pull‑request reviews.
• Design or architecture meetings where big decisions are recorded. | Ongoing – engineers flag things as they work, and the team may run a more formal internal audit **once or twice a year**. | The six “pillars” that the company cares about:
• Operational Excellence
• Security
• Reliability
• Performance Efficiency
• Cost Optimisation
• Sustainability.
Any deviation from the company’s best‑practice guidelines is logged as **technical debt** and prioritized by criticality. | **Key points** * It’s **internal** because the same people who build and run the system are the ones checking it. * The focus is on **continuous improvement** – catching small issues early, making sure architectural guardrails are respected, and keeping technical debt visible. * The team can act quickly: if a pull‑request introduces a security flaw, a reviewer can raise it immediately. --- ## 2. External audits | What they are | Who does them | How they’re done | When they happen | What they look at | |---------------|--------------|------------------|------------------|-------------------| | An independent, third‑party review of the system. | External security advisors, specialised audit firms, or partner companies that provide penetration‑testing services. | • Automated scans using **external tooling/services** that examine the code base or a non‑production copy of the live system.
• Manual security tests such as **penetration testing** performed by a partner.
• Sometimes a formal **AWS Well‑Architected Framework** audit run by the cloud provider’s own tools. | Usually **once or twice a year**, as part of the company’s compliance calendar (e.g., NIS2 requirements). | The same six pillars, but with an added emphasis on **regulatory compliance** (e.g., NIS2), **risk exposure**, and how the system measures up against industry‑wide best practices rather than just internal guidelines. Findings are reported back to the company and tracked as technical debt, just like internal findings. | **Key points** * It’s **external** because an independent party that isn’t involved in day‑to‑day development performs the check. * The goal is to get an **objective view** and to satisfy external requirements (legal, regulatory, customer contracts). * Because the reviewers are outsiders, they often spot things the internal team might have missed, especially hidden security weaknesses. --- ## 3. How the two differ | Aspect | Internal Audit | External Audit | |--------|----------------|----------------| | **Who performs it** | Your own engineers, Head of Engineering, internal security advisors. | Independent consultants, security partners, cloud‑provider audit services. | | **Scope & tools** | Uses in‑house tooling, pull‑request reviews, internal design sessions. | Uses third‑party scanning tools, manual pentests, AWS Well‑Architected self‑service audit, etc. | | **Frequency** | Continuous (daily code reviews) + formal internal review 1‑2 × a year. | Typically 1‑2 × a year, driven by compliance calendars. | | **Primary purpose** | Keep the product healthy, catch technical debt early, enforce internal guardrails. | Prove compliance, get an unbiased risk assessment, satisfy regulators or customers. | | **Outcome** | Action items are entered into the team’s backlog and prioritized by criticality. | Findings are handed over as a report; the company must address them (often with a deadline set by the auditor). | | **Cost** | Mostly internal staff time (relatively low direct cost). | Paid services, tool licences, possibly travel – higher direct cost. | --- ## 4. Why you need both Think of **internal audits** as your regular dentist check‑ups: you see the dentist (your team) frequently, so problems are caught early and can be fixed cheaply. **External audits** are more like an annual full‑body health scan at a specialist clinic: they look at the whole picture, follow strict standards, and give you a certification that you’re meeting industry or legal requirements. Having both gives you the best of both worlds: day‑to‑day quality and long‑term confidence that you’re compliant and secure. --- ### TL;DR * **Internal audits** = done by your own people, using internal tools, continuous, focused on improvement and tracking technical debt. * **External audits** = done by independent experts, using third‑party tools and manual pen‑tests, usually once or twice a year, focused on compliance and an unbiased risk view. Both feed into the same set of pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost, sustainability) and the findings from each are treated as technical debt that the team prioritises based on how critical they are. Hope that clears things up! If you have any more questions about how the audits fit into your specific workflow, just let me know.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Sure thing! VirtualQ comes with **two built‑in optimizers** that help keep the system running fast, efficient, and cost‑effective. Here’s a quick, friendly rundown of each one and what it does: | Optimizer | What it is | What it does for you | |-----------|------------|----------------------| | **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** | A rule‑based, “plug‑and‑play” optimizer that can be turned on or off with minimal setup. | • **Adjusts resources on the fly** based on current load (e.g., scaling up when traffic spikes, scaling down when things calm).
• **Keeps the system flexible** – it works well when you need a quick, reliable way to balance performance and cost without deep configuration.
• **Runs in the background** using the existing monitoring tools (Rollbar, New Relic, OpsGenie) so you don’t have to write extra code. | | **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** | A smarter, AI‑/ML‑driven optimizer that looks ahead at usage patterns. | • **Predicts future demand** by learning from historical data (training data is mentioned in the same section).
• **Proactively provisions or de‑provisions resources** before a spike or lull actually happens, which can reduce latency and avoid wasted capacity.
• **Continuously improves** as more data is collected, so its predictions get more accurate over time. | ### How they fit together - **AFO** is great for “set‑and‑forget” scenarios where you want a reliable, flexible safety net that reacts to what’s happening right now. - **APO** kicks it up a notch by **forecasting** what will happen next, letting VirtualQ stay ahead of the curve and often saving you even more on cloud costs. Both optimizers are part of VirtualQ’s broader AI/ML capabilities (you’ll also see things like speech recognition, intent recognition, and speech synthesis in the system). They’re designed to work with the same monitoring stack (Rollbar, New Relic, OpsGenie), so you can see their impact in the dashboards you already use. In short, **AFO = flexible, reactive optimization** and **APO = predictive, learning‑based optimization**—together they help VirtualQ stay fast, stable, and cost‑efficient. Let me know if you’d like a deeper dive into how to enable or tune either one!
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
Great question! When it comes to using third-party software or services at virtualQ, we have a few important legal criteria we always check to make sure everything is safe, compliant, and sustainable.

Since we handle sensitive data—especially data protected by the EU’s GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)—we need to be extra careful. Here’s what we look at:

1. **Data Privacy & Location**: We check where the service stores and processes data. If it's outside the EU, that can be a red flag. We also make sure any third-party provider can be included in our Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) with clients, because some of our customers (like those in healthcare or critical infrastructure) have very strict privacy rules.

2. **Licensing**: The software must have a license that allows us to use it commercially—even as part of a product we sell. Not all open-source licenses are OK for this, so we review them carefully.

3. **IP Ownership**: We ensure that using the software won’t create any issues with intellectual property. We don’t want surprises down the road about who owns what.

4. **Security & Maintenance**: We check if the software is actively maintained and if security updates are released promptly. We also ask: *Can someone else fix or maintain it if the original developer stops?* This helps us avoid getting stuck with outdated or unsafe tools.

In short, we make sure any third-party tool we use is legally safe, respects user privacy, and won’t put us (or our customers) at risk. It’s all about building trust and keeping data secure! 😊

Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. response:
We use a few different programming languages, depending on what part of the system we're working on:

- **Ruby and Elixir** are used for the main application logic. Most of the standard components are built with these.
- **Python** is used specifically for machine learning and AI tasks, like speech recognition, intent detection, and translation.
- For user interfaces, we use **HTML and JavaScript**, which are standard web technologies.

So, in short: **Ruby, Elixir, Python, HTML, and JavaScript** — each playing a role based on what they do best! This helps keep things efficient and maintainable.

response:
The central frameworks used in the project are **Ruby on Rails** and **React/Redux**.

Here’s a bit more detail in simple terms:

- **Ruby on Rails** is used for the backend (the server-side logic). It helps handle things like processing data, communicating with databases, and sending information to the user interface. It follows a model-view-controller (MVC) structure, which keeps the code organized and makes development faster.

- **React** and **Redux** work together on the frontend (what users see and interact with in the browser). 
  - **React** helps build reusable UI components (like buttons, forms, or entire sections of a webpage).
  - **Redux** helps manage the application’s state — for example, keeping track of user login status or form inputs across different parts of the app.

These frameworks are important because they provide the overall structure for the application, and switching them later would be a big effort. Luckily, all of these are well-supported, actively maintained, and widely used in the industry.

Great question! Let me break it down in a simple way.

**Internal audits** are checks your own team does to make sure everything in the system—like code, design, and infrastructure—is built the right way. At virtualQ, these internal reviews happen regularly and include things like:

- Code reviews (where engineers check each other’s work before it goes live)
- Design discussions within the team
- Architecture meetings for bigger decisions
- Using tools like the **AWS Well-Architected Framework**, which helps evaluate cloud setups based on best practices in areas like security, reliability, and performance

These internal checks help catch issues early and keep technical quality high. They usually happen once or twice a year for formal reviews, and findings are tracked so they can be fixed based on how important they are.

On the other hand, **external audits** are done by people or tools *outside* your company. These bring an unbiased, fresh perspective. For virtualQ, external audits include:

- Automated security scanning using third-party tools
- Manual **penetration testing** (where security experts try to find weaknesses in the system like real hackers would)
- Reviews of both the code and non-production versions of the system

These are also done regularly and help verify that the system is secure and follows standards like **NIS2** or other regulations.

👉 So the main difference is:
- **Internal audits** = done by your own team, focused on best practices and design.
- **External audits** = done by outside experts or tools, focused on real-world security and compliance.

Both are super important—they work together to keep the system safe, reliable, and well-built!
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

response:
Great question! 😊

The virtualQ system offers several different optimizers—these are basically smart algorithms that help manage and improve how callers are handled in a contact center. Here's a quick breakdown of the ones available:

1. **Flexible Optimizer (FO)** – This one adapts to changing conditions in real time, helping to adjust wait times and routing based on current call center activity.

2. **Dynamic Optimizer (DO)** – Similar to FO, it responds to live data but focuses more on dynamically updating predictions and decisions as new information comes in.

3. **Predictive Optimizer (PO)** – Uses historical data and patterns to *predict* future call volumes and wait times, helping to make smarter decisions ahead of time.

4. **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** – A more advanced version of PO that automates the use of predictive models, so less manual input is needed.

5. **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** – Combines automation with real-time flexibility, adjusting quickly to changes without needing constant oversight.

6. **Static Optimizer (SO)** – This is the simplest one. It uses fixed rules or settings and doesn’t change based on real-time or predictive data. Good for stable, predictable environments.

7. **virtualQ Algorithm (VQ)** – This is the system’s own built-in method, fine-tuned specifically for how virtualQ works, balancing speed and accuracy in wait time estimates.

Each optimizer has its strengths, and the best one for a customer depends on their specific needs—like how busy they are, how much their call volume changes, and how much automation they want.

Think of it like choosing the right tool for the job—some are better for speed, some for accuracy, and others for hands-off operation. 🛠️✨

Let me know if you'd like help picking which might be best for a certain situation!
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Hey there! I understand you're curious about the legal criteria for using 3rd party software. Let's break it down in simple terms.

When we're considering using software created by another company, we need to make sure everything is on the up and up legally. Here’s what we usually look into:

1. **Legal Compliance:** 
   - We need to ensure that the software complies with laws in our specific region. For us, this includes regulations like the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) in the EU. These laws protect personal data and make sure it's handled properly.

2. **Data Location and Privacy:**
   - We have to be very careful about where the data is stored and processed. If the software or service is run by a 3rd party, it might need to be listed in the Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) that we share with our clients. This ensures that data privacy agreements are clear.

3. **Licenses and Intellectual Property (IP):**
   - We evaluate the licenses to make sure we have the right to use the software. Also, we need to be clear about who owns the intellectual property. This is very important, especially when integrating open-source components into our system.

To sum it up, we make sure the 3rd party software won’t land us in legal trouble, that it respects data privacy laws, and that we have the necessary permissions to use it. This helps us avoid any potential legal issues down the line.

Hope that clears things up! Feel free to ask if you have more questions.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

1. **Application Logic**: We primarily use **Ruby** and **Elixir** for the core business logic of our applications. Ruby is great for its flexibility and readability, while Elixir is super powerful for handling concurrency and scalability.

2. **User Interfaces**: For the parts of our applications that users interact with, we use **HTML** and **JavaScript**. HTML builds the structure of web pages, and JavaScript makes them interactive and dynamic.

3. **Machine Learning and AI**: When it comes to advanced functionalities like machine learning and AI, we use **Python**. Python has a rich ecosystem of libraries that make it perfect for these tasks.

These choices help us balance performance, security, and maintainability. Plus, each of these languages has strong communities and organizations behind them, ensuring long-term support and regular updates.

response:
Hey there! I see you're curious about the difference between internal and external audits. Let's break it down in a way that's easy to understand.

**Internal Audits:**
- **Who’s Involved?** These are carried out by the team inside the organization, including engineers and the Head of Engineering.
- **What’s the Focus?** Internal audits focus on making sure everything is running smoothly and securely within the system. They check things like operational excellence, security, and design verification.
- **How Often?** They happen once or twice a year.
- **Decision Making:** Smaller decisions are usually done by engineers and verified in the pull request review. Bigger, strategic decisions are made in special meetings.

**External Audits:**
- **Who’s Involved?** These audits are done by outside experts or using external tools/services.
- **What’s the Focus?** They verify the system either in the code base or the live system in a non-production environment. They make sure everything meets best practices and standards.
- **How Often?** They also happen regularly, with further manual security-related audits like penetration testing done by a partner.
- **Tools and Services:** External audits may use specialized tools and services to check the system, ensuring it’s secure and optimal.

**Key Differences:**
- **Internal Audits** are more about internal checks, daily operations, and making sure everything is up to standard within the organization.
- **External Audits** provide an independent check, often using specialized tools/services to ensure there are no hidden issues and that the system meets external standards and best practices.

So, in summary, internal audits are like regular health check-ups done by your own doctor, while external audits are like getting a second opinion from another specialist. Both are important to keep everything running smoothly and securely!
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Sure thing! When we’re thinking about bringing in a 3rd‑party library, tool, or service, the **legal side** is all about making sure we stay on the right side of the law and protect both our company and our customers. Here’s a quick, friendly rundown of the key legal criteria we check:

| **Legal criterion** | **Why it matters** | **What we look for** |
|---------------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| **GDPR compliance** | We handle personal data that’s covered by the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation. | The vendor must process data in a way that meets GDPR rules (e.g., lawful basis, data‑subject rights, breach notification). |
| **Geographical location of the service** | Data stored or processed outside the EU can trigger extra safeguards. | We verify where the provider’s servers are and whether cross‑border transfers are allowed (e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses, EU‑US Data‑Privacy Framework). |
| **Data‑privacy agreements** | Our clients expect us to keep their data safe and private. | We need a solid Data Processing Agreement (DPA) that outlines responsibilities, security measures, and audit rights. |
| **Inclusion in our DPA list** | Some 3rd‑party services have to be explicitly listed in the DPAs we share with our customers. | We check that the provider can be added to that list and that the DPA terms are acceptable. |
| **License compatibility for commercial use** | We want to be able to sell the final product that includes the 3rd‑party component. | The component’s license must permit commercial exploitation—e.g., MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD are fine; GPL‑v2/v3 may be problematic unless we’re prepared to open‑source our own code. |
| **IP ownership & rights** | We must be sure we own or are licensed to use any IP that ends up in our product. | We confirm who holds the copyright/patents and that the license grants us the necessary rights (including any downstream sublicensing). |
| **Open‑source license monitoring** | Not every open‑source license is “business‑friendly.” | We maintain a curated list of approved licenses (kept up‑to‑date with legal counsel) and verify that any new library fits that list. |
| **Security‑patch obligations** | Legal risk can arise if a known vulnerability is left unpatched. | The vendor must provide timely security updates, and we need a process to apply those patches quickly. |
| **Ability for others to maintain the component** | If the original author disappears, we shouldn’t be stuck. | Good documentation and a community or support channel that allows us (or another team) to take over maintenance if needed. |

### In a nutshell

**Legal criteria for 3rd‑party software = GDPR‑friendly data handling + clear data‑privacy contracts + approved commercial‑use licenses + well‑defined IP rights + reliable security updates + maintainability.**  

We run each of these checks before we say “yes” to a new library or service, so we avoid legal headaches, protect our customers’ data, and keep the product sellable and future‑proof. Let me know if you’d like to dive deeper into any one of these points!
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

In other words, the bulk of our back‑end code is written in Ruby and Elixir, the web pages are built with HTML and made interactive with JavaScript, and all of the data‑science, model‑training, and AI‑related pieces are done in Python. Sure thing!  

The two “central frameworks” that the system (VirtualQ) relies on are:

1. **Ruby on Rails** – a Model‑View‑Controller (MVC) web framework written in Ruby. It handles the back‑end: receiving data from clients (via UI or APIs), processing it, and persisting it in the database.

2. **React + Redux** – a pair of front‑end frameworks.  
   * **React** is used to build the user‑interface components.  
   * **Redux** works alongside React to manage the application’s state (i.e., keep track of data that the UI displays and updates).

So, in short: **Ruby on Rails** for the server side, and **React together with Redux** for the client side. Those three pieces together form the core scaffolding of the application.

### What’s an **internal audit** and what’s an **external audit**? Both kinds of audits are simply “check‑ups” that make sure the virtualQ system (and the rest of our IT landscape) is built, run, and protected the right way. Think of them like health‑check‑ups for a person – one is done by the **family doctor** (people who already work for us) and the other by a **specialist you bring in from outside**. | Aspect | Internal Audit | External Audit | |--------|----------------|----------------| | **Who does it?** | People inside the company – e.g., the **Head of Engineering**, engineers, the **Chief Executive Officer**, and the **external security advisor** who works with us on a regular basis. | Independent third‑party experts or vendors that we hire for a specific review. In our case they use **external tooling/services** and a **partner that runs penetration‑tests**. | | **What’s looked at?** | • How we follow our own processes and guardrails (pull‑request reviews, design meetings, architecture sessions).
• Alignment with the **AWS Well‑Architected Framework** (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability).
• Any technical debt we’ve already identified. | • The same six pillars, but the reviewers check the **code base** and the **live (non‑production) environment** with tools they bring in.
• They also do **manual security tests** such as penetration testing. | | **How often?** | Usually **once or twice a year**, and the findings are tracked as technical debt and followed up based on how critical they are. | Also typically **once or twice a year**, but the timing can be driven by contract milestones or when we want an extra safety net before a big release. | | **Why do it?** | • Keep day‑to‑day work aligned with best practices.
• Spot issues early so engineers can fix them in the same pull‑request or sprint.
• Provide continuous improvement for the team. | • Get an **independent view** that isn’t influenced by internal politics or blind spots.
• Meet regulatory or compliance requirements (e.g., NIS2, SGB).
• Validate that our security controls really work against real‑world attackers. | | **What happens to the results?** | Findings are logged as **technical debt** and prioritized by criticality. The engineering team (or the Head of Engineering) decides how and when to fix them. | Findings are reported back to us, often with a formal **audit report**. We then create remediation plans, sometimes with the external partner’s help, and track the fixes just like internal ones. | --- ### The key differences, summed up 1. **Who’s looking?** - *Internal*: Your own team members (engineers, Head of Engineering, CEO). - *External*: Independent vendors or security partners who bring fresh eyes and specialized tools. 2. **Perspective** - *Internal* audits are great for catching everyday slip‑ups and making sure the team follows its own processes. - *External* audits are valuable for an unbiased, third‑party validation—especially important for compliance (e.g., NIS2) and for discovering hidden security gaps. 3. **Tools & Methods** - Internally we rely on **pull‑request reviews**, **architecture meetings**, and the **AWS Well‑Architected self‑service audit**. - Externally we use **third‑party tooling** that scans the code or the staging environment, plus **manual penetration testing** performed by a partner. 4. **Outcome handling** - Both produce findings, but internal findings are usually handled directly by the engineering team as part of their regular work. - External findings often come with a formal report and may require a separate remediation plan, sometimes with the external partner’s assistance. --- ### Why do we need **both**? Having **both** audits gives us a well‑rounded safety net: - **Internal audits** keep the day‑to‑day development healthy and ensure we’re continuously improving. - **External audits** give us confidence that an independent set of eyes can’t easily break into our system and that we’re meeting legal or industry standards. Together they help us stay secure, reliable, cost‑effective, and sustainable—exactly the six pillars we care about. 🚀
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Hey there! Let’s break down the two optimizers that virtualQ ships with and what each one is meant to do.

---

## 1. Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)

**What it is:**  
AFO is the “real‑time” brain of the system. It watches what’s happening right now—how many calls or chats are coming in, how many agents are free, how long people have been waiting, etc.—and then instantly tweaks the routing and resource settings to keep everything running smoothly.

**What it does:**  
| Task | How AFO helps |
|------|----------------|
| **Load‑balancing** | Moves work between queues or agents so no single line gets overloaded. |
| **Dynamic staffing** | Can trigger alerts (or even auto‑scale cloud agents) when demand spikes suddenly. |
| **Service‑level protection** | Adjusts priorities to make sure SLA targets (e.g., “answer within 30 seconds”) stay on track. |
| **Adaptability** | Because it reacts to live data, it works well even when patterns change quickly (e.g., a sudden marketing campaign). |

Think of AFO as a traffic cop who constantly watches the road and redirects cars on the fly to avoid jams.

---

## 2. Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)

**What it is:**  
APO takes a step back and looks at the *history* and *trends* instead of just the present moment. Using machine‑learning models, it forecasts how many interactions will arrive in the near future and pre‑plans the best way to handle them.

**What it does:**  
| Task | How APO helps |
|------|----------------|
| **Demand forecasting** | Predicts call/chat volume for the next hour, day, or week based on past patterns, seasonality, campaigns, etc. |
| **Proactive staffing** | Suggests how many agents (or bots) should be scheduled ahead of time so the team is ready before the surge hits. |
| **Scenario planning** | Lets managers run “what‑if” simulations (e.g., “What if we launch a new ad?”) and see the expected impact on workload. |
| **Optimization of resources** | By knowing the upcoming load, it can allocate the right mix of human agents, IVR scripts, and AI bots to keep costs low while maintaining quality. |

In other words, APO is like a weather forecast for your contact‑center traffic—it tells you what to expect so you can prepare in advance.

---

### Quick recap

| Optimizer | Main focus | How it works |
|-----------|------------|--------------|
| **AFO** (Automated Flexible Optimizer) | Real‑time adjustments | Continuously monitors live metrics and instantly re‑balances queues, agents, and routing. |
| **APO** (Automated Predictive Optimizer) | Forward‑looking planning | Analyzes historical data, predicts future volumes, and recommends staffing and configuration ahead of time. |

Both optimizers are built into the virtualQ platform, so you get the best of both worlds: **quick reactions when things change suddenly** (AFO) and **smart preparation when you can see the trend coming** (APO). Together they help keep wait times low, agent utilization high, and overall customer experience smooth. 

Hope that clears things up! If you’d like more details on how to set them up or see them in action, just let me know. 😊
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
Great question! When it comes to using third-party software or services at virtualQ, we need to be extra careful—especially because we handle sensitive data protected by strict rules like the EU’s GDPR, German social law (SGB), and requirements for critical infrastructure (KRITIS).

So, the **legal criteria** for any third-party software or service include:

1. **Data Privacy & Location**: We check where the service stores and processes data. Since we work with EU-regulated data, the software must comply with GDPR. That means no sending data to countries without proper privacy protections, and any third-party provider that handles our data may need to be listed in our Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) with clients.

2. **Licensing & Intellectual Property (IP)**: We make sure the software’s license allows us to use it commercially—and even sell our full product that includes it. Not all open-source licenses allow that, so we review them carefully.

3. **No Legal Risks**: We avoid tools that could create legal problems down the road—like those with unclear ownership, risky terms, or potential for vendor lock-in.

4. **Documentation & Maintainability**: The software should be well-documented and easy for someone else (not just the original creator) to maintain or replace if needed. This helps us avoid being stuck if the tool is abandoned.

In short: we make sure any third-party tool we use is **legal, safe, sustainable, and respects user privacy**—especially since our clients often have very high security and compliance standards. It’s all about building trust and staying on the right side of the law! 😊
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

- **Ruby and Elixir** are used for the main application logic (like handling user requests and running the core features).
- **Python** is used specifically for machine learning and AI tasks.
- For the user interfaces (what people see and interact with in the browser), we use **HTML and JavaScript**.

So, it's a mix: Ruby and Elixir for the backend, Python for data science, and HTML/JavaScript for the frontend. This helps us use the right tool for each job while keeping everything maintainable and up to date.

response:
The central frameworks used in VirtualQ are:

1. **Ruby on Rails** – This is a server-side web framework written in Ruby. It follows the Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern and helps build applications that interact with users (via websites or APIs), process data, and store it in a database. It’s been around since 2004, is widely used by big companies, actively maintained, and released about once a year. It’s also open-source under the MIT license.

2. **React / Redux** – These are frontend frameworks (or libraries) used for building user interfaces.  
   - **React** helps create reusable UI components (like buttons, forms, etc.) that update smoothly when data changes.  
   - **Redux** works alongside React to manage the application’s state — basically, it keeps track of how data changes over time as users interact with the app.

Together, Ruby on Rails handles the backend (server, database, and business logic), while React and Redux power the frontend (what users see and interact with in their browsers). These frameworks form the core foundation of the application’s structure.

response:
Great question! Let me break it down in a simple way.

**Internal audits** are checks that happen within the company, usually led by your own team — like the Head of Engineering or engineers themselves. These reviews help make sure everything is built the right way, following best practices. For example, they might look at system design, code quality, or how things are set up on AWS (using something called the *AWS Well-Architected Framework*). These audits focus on things like security, reliability, performance, and cost. If they find issues, those get recorded as "technical debt" and fixed based on how important they are. These usually happen once or twice a year.

On the other hand, **external audits** involve outside experts or tools. These could be third-party security partners who do things like *penetration testing* (basically trying to break into the system safely to find weaknesses) or using external services to scan the code or test the live system in a safe, non-production environment. This gives an unbiased, fresh look at how secure and well-built the system really is.

So, the main difference is:
- **Internal audits** = done by your own team, focused on design, architecture, and ongoing improvements.
- **External audits** = done by outside experts, focused on security and validation using real-world attack methods or tools.

Both are super helpful — internal ones help you improve continuously, while external ones give you that extra layer of trust and verification from outside eyes. 😊
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Great question! 😊

virtualQ offers several different optimizers—these are smart algorithms designed to help manage and improve the caller experience in contact centers by estimating or managing how long people might have to wait on hold.

Here are the main optimizers available in the virtualQ system:

1. **Flexible Optimizer (FO):** This one is great for adapting to changing call volumes. It adjusts wait time predictions dynamically based on real-time conditions, making it flexible (as the name suggests!) for different situations.

2. **Dynamic Optimizer (DO):** Similar to FO, this optimizer uses live data to continuously update wait times. It’s ideal when you want the system to automatically respond to sudden spikes or drops in call traffic.

3. **Predictive Optimizer (PO):** This optimizer uses historical data to forecast wait times more accurately. It "learns" from past patterns—like busy times of day or days of the week—to predict what’s coming.

4. **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO):** A more advanced version of PO, APO automates much of the setup and tuning process. It combines historical trends with real-time data and requires less manual input, making it easier to use at scale.

5. **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO):** This blends automation with adaptability. It adjusts to current call center conditions automatically while staying flexible enough to handle unexpected changes.

6. **Static Optimizer (SO):** This is the simplest option. It uses fixed rules or average wait times and doesn’t change much based on real-time data. It's useful for smaller or less complex contact centers where things don’t change too quickly.

7. **virtualQ Algorithm (VQ):** This is the core algorithm built specifically for the virtualQ system. It combines multiple data points to give a balanced and reliable wait time estimate.

So in short—each optimizer works a little differently, and virtualQ lets you choose the one that best fits your contact center’s needs. Some are more automated, some rely on history, and others react in real time. The goal? To keep callers happy and operations running smoothly! 🎯📞

Let me know if you’d like help picking the right one for your situation!
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Hey there! I see you're curious about the legal criteria for using 3rd party software. Let's break it down in a way that's easy to understand.

**Legal Criteria for 3rd Party Software:**

1. **Data Privacy and Compliance:**
   - **EU’s GDPR:** We need to make sure the 3rd party software complies with the General Data Protection Regulation. This means they must protect any personal data we share with them.
   - **Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB):** If we're dealing with customers regulated under the German social code, the software must meet those specific requirements too.
   - **KRITIS:** For critical infrastructure, the software must adhere to stringent standards to ensure it won’t cause big problems if something goes wrong.

2. **Geographical Location:**
   - The location where the software's services and data are stored is very important. We have to ensure that our data isn't being accessed from regions with different privacy laws, which might not be as strict.

3. **Data Privacy Agreements:**
   - We need to carefully review any data privacy agreements. This is especially important for services provided by third-party providers, as they might need to be listed on our Data Protection Agreements (DPAs).

4. **Licenses and IP Ownership:**
   - The software must come with clear licenses and ownership details. This is crucial, especially if it includes open-source components, because not every open-source license allows for the same use.

So, in short, when choosing 3rd party software, we're making sure it's legally sound, protects our information, and aligns with all regulatory requirements. This way, we avoid any legal issues and ensure our data remains secure. Hope that helps!
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

Hi there! I'm glad you asked about the differences between internal and external audits. Let's break it down in a simple way.

**Internal Audits:**

These are audits conducted by your own team, usually the engineers and the Head of Engineering. They review the internal workings of your systems and processes. Here's what they typically include:

- **Focus on Best Practices:** Internal audits check if your team's processes and designs follow best practices.
- **Frequent Checks:** They are done regularly, often once or twice a year.
- **Track Findings:** The findings (like areas where improvements are needed) are tracked as "technical debt" and addressed based on their importance.
- **Review in Meetings:** Smaller decisions and checks are done during pull request reviews. Bigger, strategic decisions need dedicated meetings.

**External Audits:**

These audits are done by outside experts or third-party services, often with specialized tools or services. Here’s what they usually involve:

- **Verification with Tools:** External tools and services verify the code base or the live system in a non-production environment.
- **Penetration Testing:** Apart from using tools, external audits also include manual security-related audits such as penetration testing, carried out by a partner.
- **Broader Focus:** External audits may look at things from a broader perspective, ensuring that your systems meet industry standards.

In summary, **internal audits** are conducted by your own team and focus on best practices and regular checks, while **external audits** are done by outside experts using tools and services and often include more comprehensive security checks. Both aim to improve your systems but from different angles and using different methods. Hope this helps clarify things! If you have more questions, feel free to ask. 😊
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

Great question! Let's dive into the optimizers that virtualQ offers. 

VirtualQ provides two different types of optimizers to improve and fine-tune their system: the Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO) and the Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO).

1. **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)**:
   - This optimizer helps make the system more adaptable. It allows the system to adjust and respond to different conditions and requirements as needed. Think of it as the part of the system that can tweak and fine-tune processes on the fly to better fit specific situations.

2. **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)**:
   - This optimizer is all about looking ahead. It uses data and patterns to predict what might happen next and prepares the system to handle those situations efficiently. Imagine it as a smart assistant that anticipates needs and gets everything ready in advance.

So, in summary, both optimizers work together to make the virtualQ system smarter and more efficient, but in different ways. The AFO focuses on flexibility and the APO on prediction and preparation. These tools help ensure that the system runs smoothly and effectively.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

Hey there! It looks like you're asking about the best new graphic cards we offer. However, based on the information you've provided, it seems we're actually diving into details about our forecasting engines, simulation engines, and optimization algorithms.

If you're interested in graphic cards, it might be a bit outside the scope of our current conversation which is about system capabilities and optimization technologies. Our main focus here is on how our systems can be scaled, the various algorithms we use like the Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO), and our machine learning/AI features.

If you’re looking for information specifically on graphic cards, I’d recommend checking out our latest product intelligence or the product roadmap under "Features and Capabilities Overview." This should give you a clear picture of the latest tech we have to offer.

Sure thing! When you’re thinking about bringing a 3rd‑party library, tool, or service into a product like virtualQ, the **legal side** is one of the first things you check. Here’s a simple, bite‑size checklist of the main legal criteria you’ll want to run through:

| ✅ Legal Criterion | What it means (in plain language) | Why it matters for virtualQ |
|-------------------|------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| **GDPR compliance** | The software must respect the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation – e.g., it can’t store or move personal data in a way that breaks the rules. | virtualQ handles regulated data, so any third‑party that can see that data must be GDPR‑safe. |
| **Geo‑location of the service** | Know where the servers that run the software live (EU, US, etc.). Some jurisdictions have stricter data‑privacy laws. | If the service runs outside the EU, you may need extra safeguards or may be barred from using it. |
| **Data‑privacy agreements & DPAs** | A Data Processing Agreement (DPA) spells out who does what with the data. The 3rd‑party must be willing to be listed in virtualQ’s DPAs that are shared with clients. | Clients (especially public‑sector ones) often demand that every processor be documented. |
| **License type & commercial‑use rights** | The software’s license must explicitly allow you to **use it in a commercial product and resell that product**. Open‑source licenses vary – some (e.g., GPL) may require you to open‑source your own code, others (MIT, Apache 2.0) are more permissive. | virtualQ sells its solution, so a “non‑commercial only” or “viral” license would be a deal‑breaker. |
| **IP ownership & rights** | You need clear ownership or at least a granted right to use any patents, trademarks, or copyrighted parts that the component contains. | Prevents future lawsuits that could force you to stop selling the product or pay hefty damages. |
| **Security‑patch policy** | The provider must have a documented process for delivering security updates quickly (ideally “as soon as possible”). | Keeping data safe is both a legal and operational requirement, especially under GDPR’s “security by design” principle. |
| **Documentation & maintainability** | The component should be well‑documented, and you (or someone else) must be able to maintain it without being locked into the original vendor. | Avoids lock‑in and ensures you can keep the system running even if the vendor disappears or stops supporting the product. |
| **End‑of‑Life (EoL) & lock‑in considerations** | Check the roadmap: is the software still actively maintained? Will it be discontinued soon? | If the tool disappears, you could be left with a non‑functional piece of your product, which is a legal risk (you can’t deliver what you promised to customers). |
| **Compliance with sector‑specific rules** | For customers under the German Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB) or KRITIS (critical infrastructure) regulations, the software may need to meet additional standards set by the Federal Office for IT Security (BSI). | Those customers can’t accept a component that doesn’t meet their stricter rules. |

### How you actually use this checklist

1. **Start with the license** – read the fine print. If the license says “commercial use prohibited” or forces you to open‑source your own code, cross it off.
2. **Ask for the DPA** – the vendor should be willing to sign a Data Processing Agreement that matches virtualQ’s template.
3. **Verify GDPR & location** – look at where the data lives and whether the vendor has GDPR certifications or documented compliance measures.
4. **Check security updates** – ask for their patch‑release cadence and whether they have a public CVE‑track record.
5. **Confirm documentation** – skim the API docs, user guides, and see if there’s a community or support channel that can help you later.
6. **Look at the roadmap** – is there a clear end‑of‑life policy? Is the product still getting new releases?

If a component passes all of these boxes, you can feel confident that you’re not stepping into a legal minefield, you can sell your product without restrictions, and you’ll stay on the right side of GDPR and other sector‑specific regulations.

**Bottom line:** the legal criteria boil down to **(1) data‑privacy compliance (GDPR, DPAs, geo‑location), (2) licensing that lets you use and sell the software commercially, (3) clear IP rights, (4) a reliable security‑patch process, and (5) documentation/maintenance that avoids lock‑in or dead‑ends**. Running each of those checks will help you pick safe, sustainable third‑party software for virtualQ.

Sure thing! Here’s a quick rundown of the languages that make up our codebase:

| Language | Rough share of the codebase | What we mainly use it for |
|----------|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Ruby** | ~43 % | Core application logic (the “brain” of the system). |
| **Elixir** | ~7 % | Also part of the core logic – it’s a functional cousin of Ruby that we use for some of the newer services. |
| **HTML / JavaScript** | ~24 % | Everything you see on the screen – the user‑interface and front‑end behavior. |
| **Python** | ~11 % | Machine‑learning, AI, and data‑science pieces. |
| **.NET / C#** | ~9 % | Legacy connectors (the older ACD pieces that we still maintain). |
| **Other (e.g., Terraform templates)** | ~6 % | Infrastructure‑as‑code and a few supporting scripts. |

So, in short, our stack is built around **Ruby and Elixir for the back‑end logic**, **HTML/JavaScript for the front‑end**, and **Python for the data‑science/AI work**, with a smaller amount of **.NET/C#** for legacy bits and some **Terraform** for infrastructure. Hope that helps!

### What’s an audit, anyway?

Think of an audit as a “check‑up” for a system or a process. Just like you go to the doctor for a health exam, a company runs audits to see whether everything is working the way it should, to spot problems early, and to make sure they’re following the rules they’ve set (or that regulators have set).

---

## Internal audits – the “in‑house” health check

**Who does it?**  
People who already work at the company – in your case the Head of Engineering, the engineers themselves, and sometimes a dedicated internal audit team.

**What do they look at?**  

| Area | Typical activities |
|------|--------------------|
| **Design & Architecture** | Review of code, pull‑request checks, internal design‑verification meetings. |
| **Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance, Cost, Sustainability** | The six “pillars” the audit framework uses to judge the system. |
| **Technical debt** | Anything that diverges from best practice is logged as technical debt and then prioritized by how critical it is. |
| **Frequency** | Usually once or twice a year, but smaller checks (e.g., PR reviews) happen all the time. |

**Why do it?**  

* Catch problems early before they become costly fixes.  
* Keep the team aligned on the same architectural guardrails.  
* Track improvements as “technical debt” so you can see progress over time.

**A quick example from your setup:**  
Your internal audit team might run a review of the **virtualQ** system’s data‑flow diagrams and compare them against the internal design guidelines. If they spot a mismatch (say, a missing encryption step), they log it, assign a priority, and the engineers fix it in the next sprint.

---

## External audits – the “outside‑expert” health check

**Who does it?**  
People or services that are **not** part of your day‑to‑day team. This can be:

* A security partner that does penetration testing.  
* A third‑party tooling service that scans your code base or live (non‑production) environment.  
* Cloud‑provider tools like the **AWS Well‑Architected Framework** self‑service audit.

**What do they look at?**  

| Area | Typical activities |
|------|--------------------|
| **Tool‑based scans** | Automated checks of the code repository or the running system (e.g., vulnerability scanners, configuration checkers). |
| **Pen‑testing** | Manual “ethical hacking” performed by a partner to try to break into the system. |
| **Compliance** | Verification that you meet external standards (e.g., NIS2, ISO 27001, industry‑specific regulations). |
| **AWS Well‑Architected Review** | Looks at the same six pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability) but from the cloud‑provider’s perspective. |
| **Frequency** | Usually scheduled 1–2 times a year, but some tools can run continuously. |

**Why do it?**  

* **Objectivity** – An outside set of eyes can see things insiders might miss because they’re used to the system.  
* **Regulatory compliance** – Certain laws (like the EU’s NIS2 directive) require an independent audit to prove you’re meeting security standards.  
* **Credibility** – A clean external audit report can be a selling point for customers, partners, or investors.

**A quick example from your setup:**  
Your partner security firm might run a penetration test against the **virtualQ** system in a staging environment. They could discover, for instance, that an API endpoint is vulnerable to injection attacks—something the internal team hadn’t caught. The finding is then fed back into your internal technical‑debt backlog for remediation.

---

## The key differences at a glance

| Aspect | Internal Audit | External Audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Who performs it** | Employees, internal audit team, engineers | Third‑party vendors, independent security firms, cloud‑provider tools |
| **Perspective** | “Inside view” – knows the day‑to‑day quirks, business context | “Outside view” – unbiased, often more focused on standards & best‑practice |
| **Tooling** | Pull‑request reviews, internal dashboards, internal design sessions | Automated scanners, pen‑testing services, AWS Well‑Architected tool |
| **Primary goals** | Continuous improvement, tracking technical debt, aligning teams | Compliance, external validation, uncover hidden risks |
| **Frequency** | Ongoing (PR reviews) + 1–2 formal reviews per year | Usually 1–2 formal reviews per year, but some tools run continuously |
| **Outcome** | Action items fed into the team’s backlog; internal metrics | Formal audit report, compliance certifications, recommendations for remediation |

---

### Bottom line

Both types of audits are essential. **Internal audits** keep the ship sailing smoothly day‑to‑day, letting your engineers catch and fix issues as part of their regular work. **External audits** act like a fresh set of doctors checking the whole body, ensuring you meet industry standards, spotting blind‑spot vulnerabilities, and giving you that extra layer of confidence for regulators and customers.

Running both in tandem gives you a robust, continuously improving system that’s both **secure** and **aligned with best practices**. 🚀
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

- Ensuring the software's license allows virtualQ to use it commercially, including the right to sell the whole product.
- Evaluating licenses and intellectual property (IP) ownership, especially when integrating open source components.
- Confirming that the software complies with data privacy regulations, particularly the EU’s GDPR, given the regulated nature of the data handled.
- Considering data privacy agreements, especially for services provided by third-party providers, as they may need to be included in Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) with virtualQ’s clients.
- Assessing the geographic location of services and ensuring that any potential access to data by third parties is minimized, particularly for customers with high privacy requirements (e.g., those regulated under SGB or KRITIS).
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits are self-assessments conducted within the organization, such as using the AWS Well-Architected Framework to evaluate cloud or hybrid infrastructure. These audits focus on six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability. They are carried out once or twice a year, with findings tracked as technical debt and addressed based on criticality. Participants include the Head of Engineering and internal teams, and architectural or strategic decisions are made in dedicated internal meetings or design sessions.

External audits involve verification of the virtualQ system using external tools or services, either at the code base level or on the live system in a non-production stage. They also include manual security assessments such as penetration testing conducted by an external partner. 

The main difference lies in the scope and conduct: internal audits are organization-led evaluations focusing on best practices and operational health, while external audits rely on third-party tools and experts to validate system security and integrity.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

virtualQ offers the following optimizers:

1. **Flexible Optimizer (FO)** – Used for peak management.
2. **Dynamic Optimizer (DO)** – Used for peak management and requires a data connection.
3. **Predictive Optimizer (PO)** – Used for peak management and requires a data connection.
4. **virtualQ Algorithm (VQ)** – Used for waiting time calculation and requires a data connection.
5. **Static Optimizer (SO)** – Used for waiting time calculation.

These optimizers are algorithms or strategies that help determine caller waiting times in an ACD and contact center environment. The choice of optimizer depends on the customer's optimization goal (such as peak management or waiting time calculation) and the availability of data.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

The legal criteria for 3rd party software, as outlined in the provided context, include the following:

1. **Data Privacy Agreements**: Data privacy agreements need to be carefully considered, especially for services run by 3rd party service providers. These services might have to be listed in the Data Protection Authorities (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
   
2. **Licenses and IP Ownership**: Licenses and intellectual property (IP) ownership are evaluated, particularly when integrating open-source components into the virtualQ system.

3. **Compliance with EU Data Privacy Laws**: The 3rd party software must comply with EU data privacy laws, including GDPR and the CISPE code of conduct.

These criteria ensure that the use of 3rd party software does not lead to legal issues and maintains compliance with relevant data privacy regulations.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.
