Sure thing! When we talk about the **central frameworks** that power VirtualQ, we’re referring to the two main “skeletons” that the whole system is built on:

| Framework | What it is | Why it matters for VirtualQ |
|-----------|------------|----------------------------|
| **Ruby on Rails** | A full‑stack, Model‑View‑Controller (MVC) web framework written in Ruby. | It handles the heavy lifting of receiving data from users (through UI screens or APIs), processing that data, and persisting it in the database. Because Rails already gives you conventions for routing, models, views, and controllers, developers can spin up new features quickly and keep the codebase tidy. |
| **Elixir (Phoenix)** *(the other core framework)* | Phoenix is the most common web framework for the Elixir language. It follows a similar MVC pattern but is built on the BEAM VM, which excels at handling many simultaneous connections with very low latency. | VirtualQ uses Phoenix for the parts of the system that need high‑throughput, real‑time communication (e.g., live updates, chat‑style interactions, or any feature that benefits from Elixir’s concurrency). It complements Ruby on Rails by taking care of the “real‑time” side of things while still giving developers a clean, opinionated structure. |

### In plain language
- **Ruby on Rails** = the “classic” web‑app backbone. Think of it as the well‑organized office where most of the paperwork (data entry, storage, business rules) gets done.
- **Phoenix (Elixir)** = the “high‑speed, always‑on” department. It’s perfect for handling lots of users at once and keeping things responsive in real time.

Together, these two frameworks give VirtualQ a solid, maintainable foundation for both the regular web‑app functionality and the more demanding, real‑time features. If you ever hear the term “central frameworks” in the VirtualQ docs, just remember: **Ruby on Rails + Phoenix (Elixir)**.

### Internal vs. external audits – what’s the difference? Both kinds of audits are checks that make sure the **virtualQ** system (or any other IT product) is built, run, and maintained the right way. Think of an audit like a health‑check for your software and the surrounding processes. The main thing that sets them apart is **who does the checking** and **what they focus on**. --- ## 1. Internal audits | What it is | Who does it | How it’s done | When it happens | What it looks at | |------------|------------|---------------|----------------|-----------------| | A review performed **by people inside the organisation** (e.g., the Head of Engineering, the Chief Executive Officer, the internal security team). | Employees, internal architects, design‑review groups, sometimes an internal audit team. | Walk‑throughs of code, design sessions, architecture reviews, and data‑flow diagrams. | Typically **once or twice a year**, but can be triggered by a major change or a finding. | • Operational Excellence
• Security
• Reliability
• Performance / Efficiency
• Cost Optimisation
• Sustainability
Any deviation from the company’s own best‑practice guidelines is logged as “technical debt” and tracked by its criticality. | | **Why it matters** | • Gives the team direct control over the process.
• Helps catch issues early, before they become big problems.
• Encourages continuous improvement because the same people who build the system also check it. | ### Typical internal‑audit activities in the virtualQ context * **Architecture & design sessions** – the engineering team walks through the system’s blueprint and asks, “Does this follow our design standards?” * **Internal reviews** – code‑review tools, static analysis, and manual checks on the live (non‑production) environment. * **Tracking technical debt** – every finding is recorded, prioritised, and assigned to a sprint or a roadmap item. --- ## 2. External audits | What it is | Who does it | How it’s done | When it happens | What it looks at | |------------|------------|---------------|----------------|-----------------| | An **independent assessment** performed by people or tools **outside the organisation**. | External security advisors, specialised audit firms, third‑party tooling services, penetration‑testing partners. | • Automated scans of the code base or the live (non‑production) system using external tools.
• Manual penetration testing and other hands‑on security checks carried out by a partner.
• Review of compliance with regulations such as **NIS2** (EU’s Network‑and‑Information‑Security directive). | Usually **once or twice a year**, often aligned with compliance calendars or contract requirements. | • Security (vulnerabilities, attack surface, compliance gaps).
• Alignment with industry‑wide best practices and standards (e.g., NIS2, ISO 27001).
• Objective view of how the system would appear to an attacker or regulator. | | **Why it matters** | • Provides an unbiased, third‑party perspective.
• Helps satisfy legal or regulatory obligations (e.g., NIS2).
• Can uncover blind spots that internal teams might miss because they’re too close to the code. | ### Typical external‑audit activities in the virtualQ context * **Tool‑based verification** – a vendor runs their scanner against the virtualQ code repository or a staging environment and reports any issues. * **Penetration testing** – a security partner tries to “break in” to the system, looking for weaknesses an attacker could exploit. * **Compliance check** – the auditor maps findings to NIS2 requirements, ensuring the organisation meets the EU’s cyber‑security rules. --- ## 3. Key differences at a glance | Aspect | Internal audit | External audit | |--------|----------------|----------------| | **Who performs it** | Employees, internal teams (Head of Engineering, security staff, etc.) | Independent third parties, external security advisors, specialised tooling providers | | **Perspective** | Insider view – knows the day‑to‑day processes, business constraints | Outsider view – brings fresh eyes, no “internal bias” | | **Primary focus** | Overall health of the system across all pillars (operational excellence, cost, sustainability, etc.) | Security, regulatory compliance, and validation against industry‑wide best practices | | **Tooling** | Internal static‑analysis tools, design reviews, internal dashboards | Commercial vulnerability scanners, external penetration‑testing suites | | **Objectivity** | High, but may miss blind spots because the team is familiar with the system | Very high – the auditor has no vested interest in the product | | **Regulatory relevance** | Helpful for internal governance | Often required to prove compliance with standards like NIS2 | | **Frequency** | Usually scheduled internally (once/twice a year) but can be ad‑hoc | Usually scheduled (once/twice a year) to satisfy contracts or regulations | | **Outcome** | List of technical debt items, improvement tickets, internal action plans | Formal audit report, security findings, compliance statements, sometimes remediation deadlines | --- ## 4. How they work together Think of internal and external audits as two complementary lenses: * **Internal audits** keep the day‑to‑day ship sailing smoothly. They catch small inefficiencies, ensure the team follows its own style guides, and help prioritize technical debt. * **External audits** act as a safety inspection. They make sure the ship meets legal safety standards and can survive a storm (i.e., a cyber‑attack). When both are performed regularly, the organisation gets a **full picture**: continuous improvement from inside and confidence from the outside. --- ### Quick recap for you * **Internal audit** = done by your own people → focuses on all pillars, tracks technical debt, runs often, very familiar with the system. * **External audit** = done by outsiders → focuses mainly on security and compliance (e.g., NIS2), uses third‑party tools, provides an unbiased view, and is often required for regulatory reasons. Both are essential, and together they help keep the virtualQ system reliable, secure, efficient, and compliant. If you need to set up a new audit cycle, start by defining who will lead the internal review and then line up an external partner that can cover the security/compliance side. Happy auditing!

Hey there! Let’s walk through the different “optimizers” that virtualQ offers and what each one is built to do. I’ll keep it simple and give you a quick picture of when you’d pick each one.

---

## 1. The two **automated families**  

| Optimizer family | What it is | When it shines |
|------------------|------------|----------------|
| **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** | A rule‑based engine that reacts to the *current* situation. It looks at the data that’s coming in right now (e.g., how many callers are in the queue, how many agents are free) and makes quick, on‑the‑fly decisions about when to offer a callback. | You have good real‑time data but not a lot of historic data, or you need a fast, “reactive” solution that can adapt instantly to sudden spikes. |
| **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** | A machine‑learning‑powered engine that *forecasts* the future. It trains on past call‑volume patterns, holidays, marketing campaigns, etc., and then predicts the best moments to schedule callbacks ahead of time. | You have a solid history of call data and want to plan callbacks in advance, smoothing out peaks before they even happen. |

Think of AFO as “respond now” and APO as “plan ahead”.

---

## 2. The **goal‑oriented algorithms** (the “letters” you saw in the doc)

These are the actual optimisation algorithms that live inside the AFO/APO families. Which one you use depends on **what you’re trying to optimise** and **what data you have**.

| Algorithm | Goal it solves | Typical use case |
|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| **FO – Flexible Optimizer** | **Peak management** – spreads the load during busy periods. | You want to keep the queue from blowing up during a sudden call surge, but you don’t need a full‑blown forecast. |
| **DO – Demand Optimizer** | **Peak management** – uses *real‑time demand* data (e.g., current call arrival rate). | You have a live feed of call‑arrival statistics and want the system to react instantly. |
| **PO – Predictive Optimizer** | **Peak management** – relies on *forecasted* demand. | You have historic data and want the system to schedule callbacks before the peak hits. |
| **VQ – VirtualQ Optimizer** | **Waiting‑time calculation** – figures out the *best* callback time to keep the *perceived* wait short. | Your main KPI is “average waiting time” and you want callbacks offered at moments that feel quickest to the caller. |
| **SO – Service Optimizer** | **Waiting‑time calculation** – similar to VQ but tuned for service‑level agreements (e.g., “90 % of callers answered within 2 min”). | You have strict service‑level targets and need the optimizer to respect those while still offering callbacks. |

### How they fit together

- **Peak‑management group** (FO, DO, PO) is all about *when* the call centre is busiest and how to smooth that load.  
  - **FO** is flexible and works with whatever data you have.  
  - **DO** leans on *current* demand data.  
  - **PO** leans on *predicted* demand data.

- **Waiting‑time group** (VQ, SO) is about *how long a caller feels they’re waiting*. They decide the exact callback slot that will make the caller’s experience feel fastest, either in a general sense (VQ) or with strict SLA constraints (SO).

---

## 3. Choosing the right one for you

1. **What’s your main goal?**  
   - **Smooth peaks / avoid overload?** → Look at FO, DO, or PO.  
   - **Minimise perceived wait time?** → VQ or SO.

2. **What data do you have?**  
   - **Only live data (no history)?** → DO (or FO if you want a more generic rule‑set).  
   - **Historical data + forecasting capability?** → PO (and that naturally lives inside the APO family).

3. **Do you prefer a reactive or a predictive approach?**  
   - **Reactive** → AFO + FO/DO.  
   - **Predictive** → APO + PO (or VQ/SO if you’re focusing on wait‑time).

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Optimizer | Reactive or Predictive? | Best for… |
|-----------|------------------------|-----------|
| **AFO + FO** | Reactive | Simple, fast load‑balancing when you just need “keep the queue moving”. |
| **AFO + DO** | Reactive | Real‑time demand spikes (e.g., a marketing blast that’s already happening). |
| **APO + PO** | Predictive | Planning callbacks a few minutes/hours ahead based on forecasted call volume. |
| **VQ** | Either (usually predictive) | Minimising the *perceived* wait for the caller. |
| **SO** | Either (usually predictive) | Hitting strict service‑level targets while still offering callbacks. |

---

### Bottom line

virtualQ gives you a toolbox:

- **Two engine families** (AFO = react now, APO = plan ahead).  
- **Five algorithm flavors** (FO, DO, PO for peak‑management; VQ, SO for waiting‑time).  

Pick the combination that matches your business goal and the data you can feed the system, and virtualQ will automatically schedule callbacks in the smartest possible way.

Hope that clears things up! If you have a specific scenario (e.g., “we have 3 months of call history and a daily marketing blast”), let me know and I can suggest the exact optimizer combo that would work best. 😊
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

- **Data privacy and geo-location of services**: Given that virtualQ handles data regulated by the EU’s GDPR, the geographic location of services and their data privacy practices are carefully considered. This is especially important for services provided by third-party providers, as they may need to be listed in the Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.

- **Licenses and IP ownership**: Licenses are critically evaluated, particularly when integrating open source components into the virtualQ system, as not all open source licenses are suitable for commercial use. virtualQ maintains and regularly updates a list of permissible licenses in consultation with legal experts.

- **IP ownership considerations**: This is especially relevant in contexts like generative AI, where intellectual property rights can be complex and are closely monitored to avoid legal risks.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

Internal audits are conducted through internal reviews, architecture and design sessions within the team, and internal verification of the system design. They focus on evaluating the system from within the organization using internal expertise and processes.

External audits involve the use of external tools or services to verify the virtualQ system, either in the code base or in a non-production version of the live system. Additionally, external manual security audits such as penetration testing are carried out by a partner. These audits provide an independent assessment of the system's security and functionality.

The main difference is that internal audits rely on internal processes and personnel, while external audits use third-party tools, services, and partners to provide an objective evaluation.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

1. **GDPR Compliance**: The software must comply with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), especially when handling regulated data that involves data privacy.

2. **Data Privacy Agreements**: Data privacy agreements are carefully considered, especially for services run by third-party service providers that might need to be listed in the Data Protection Agreements (DPAs).

3. **Licenses and IP Ownership**: The software must come with licenses that allow virtualQ to use them in a commercial way, including the ability to sell the whole product. 

4. **Licensing for Open Source Components**: When integrating open-source components, the licenses must allow for commercial use and should ensure that security patches are applied promptly.

5. **Documentation and Maintenance**: The component should be well-documented, and maintenance should be possible by someone other than the owner to ensure sustainability and support.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits and external audits are both crucial for assessing the virtualQ system, but they differ in their methods and participants.

**Internal Audits:**
- Internal audits are conducted by the team, including the Head of Engineering and architects.
- These audits involve internal reviews and architecture and design sessions.
- Internal audits focus on six different pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
- The purpose is to identify discrepancies from best practices and track findings as technical debt.
- These audits are carried out once or twice a year.

**External Audits:**
- External audits are based on external tooling/services that verify the virtualQ system, either in the code base or the live system in a non-production stage.
- Manual security-related audits (penetration testing) are conducted by a partner.
- External audits also focus on the same six pillars and aim to detect where the implementation diverges from best practices.
- Findings are tracked and followed up on according to their criticality.

**Differences:**
- Internal audits are conducted by internal teams and partners, while external audits are performed by external tooling/services and partners.
- Internal audits include architecture and design sessions, whereas external audits rely on external tools/services for verification.
- Both types of audits focus on the same six pillars but are conducted by different groups with potentially different perspectives.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

virtualQ offers the following optimizers:

1. **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)**
2. **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)**

The decision on which optimizer is the best fit for a specific customer situation is strongly dependent on the optimization goal a customer is aiming at or the data available to the algorithms. These optimizers are classified by optimization goals such as peak management (FO, DO, PO) or waiting time calculation (VQ, SO).
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

**Legal criteria for using 3rd‑party software (as defined in the document)**  

1. **GDPR compliance** – the library or service must respect the EU General Data Protection Regulation and any related data‑privacy obligations.  

2. **Geo‑location of the service** – where the service is hosted and processed must be acceptable for the regulated data (e.g., EU‑based or otherwise approved locations).  

3. **Data‑privacy agreements** – the provider’s privacy terms must be compatible with virtualQ’s own DPAs (Data Processing Agreements) that are shared with its clients.  

4. **Inclusion in DPAs** – any 3rd‑party service that could handle personal data may need to be listed explicitly in the DPAs that virtualQ maintains with its customers.  

5. **License suitability** – the software’s licence must:  
   * Permit commercial use,  
   * Allow virtualQ to incorporate the component into its product and sell the whole solution, and  
   * Not impose restrictions that conflict with virtualQ’s business model.  

6. **IP ownership verification** – it must be clear who owns the intellectual property and that virtualQ obtains the necessary rights to use, modify, and distribute the component.  

7. **Special‑regulation compliance** – for customers subject to additional rules (e.g., Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB), KRITIS, or requirements from the Federal Office for IT Security), the 3rd‑party software must be able to meet those higher‑level security and compliance demands.  

8. **Security‑patch management** – the provider must apply security patches promptly so that the component remains safe for use in critical or regulated environments.  

9. **Maintainability** – the component should be well documented and capable of being maintained by parties other than the original owner, ensuring that virtualQ is not locked‑in to a single vendor.  

These points together form the legal checklist that virtualQ uses before adopting any external library, tool, or service.

All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
**Internal audits**  
- Conducted by the organisation’s own staff (e.g., Head of Engineering and the internal review team).  
- Focus on *design verification* and internal reviews of the virtualQ system.  
- Follow the same six‑pillar framework (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability) and are scheduled once or twice a year.  
- Findings are recorded as technical debt and tracked for remediation according to their criticality.

**External audits**  
- Performed by third‑party services or partners.  
- Use *external tooling/services* to verify the virtualQ system either in the code base or in a non‑production version of the live system.  
- Include manual security‑related audits such as penetration testing carried out by an external partner.  
- Also follow the six‑pillar audit framework, with results similarly tracked as technical debt.

**Key differences**  
| Aspect | Internal audit | External audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Who performs it** | Internal staff (Head of Engineering, internal reviewers) | External tooling/services and external partners (e.g., penetration‑testing firm) |
| **Scope/Method** | Design verification, internal reviews | Code‑base or non‑production system checks, manual security testing |
| **Perspective** | Inside‑view of the system | Outside‑view, independent validation |
| **Purpose** | Ensure internal processes and designs meet best practices | Validate the system against external standards and uncover security issues that may not be visible internally |
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

**Optimizers provided by the virtualQ platform**

| Optimizer | Primary purpose (what it does) |
|-----------|--------------------------------|
| **Flexible Optimizer (FO)** | Used for **peak‑management** – it flexibly allocates resources to handle high‑traffic periods. |
| **Dynamic Optimizer (DO)** | Adjusts resources **dynamically** based on real‑time data; it requires a data connection to the contact‑center system. |
| **Predictive Optimizer (PO)** | **Predicts** future call‑volume patterns and provisions capacity ahead of time; also needs contact‑center data. |
| **virtualQ Algorithm (VQ)** | Calculates the **waiting time** that callers will experience; it is applied when the goal is to estimate or manage queue times. |
| **Static Optimizer (SO)** | Provides a **static** (non‑changing) configuration for waiting‑time calculation; it does not rely on live data feeds. |
| **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** | An automated version of the Flexible Optimizer that applies the same peak‑management logic without manual intervention. |
| **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** | An automated version of the Predictive Optimizer that runs predictive capacity‑planning automatically. |

**How the choice is made**  
The “best‑fit” optimizer for a customer depends on two factors that the platform highlights:

1. **Optimization goal** – e.g., managing peaks (FO, DO, PO) vs. calculating waiting time (VQ, SO).  
2. **Data connection available** – some optimizers (DO, PO, VQ) need real‑time contact‑center data, while others (SO) can operate with static data.

Thus, virtualQ offers a suite of optimizers that can be selected based on the customer’s specific performance goal and the data they have available.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

- Ensuring compliance with data privacy regulations, especially considering that the data is regulated by the EU’s GDPR.
- Carefully evaluating the geo-location of services and their data privacy agreements, particularly for services provided by third-party service providers, as they may need to be listed in the Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
- Assessing licenses and intellectual property (IP) ownership, especially when integrating open source components into the virtualQ system, since not all open source licenses are suitable for commercial use.
- Maintaining and regularly updating a list of approved licenses in consultation with legal experts.
- Monitoring IP ownership issues, particularly in emerging areas such as generative AI.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits involve reviews and evaluations conducted within the organization, including architecture and design sessions, team discussions, and internal verification of system design and implementation. These audits aim to ensure alignment with best practices and identify areas for improvement. Participants typically include internal roles such as the Chief Executive Officer and Head of Engineering.

External audits are based on assessments performed by external parties using tooling or services to verify the virtualQ system, either at the code level or in a non-production environment. They also include manual security-related evaluations such as penetration testing carried out by a partner. These audits focus on six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability, and are conducted once or twice a year. Findings are tracked as technical debt and addressed based on criticality.

The key difference lies in the auditor's affiliation: internal audits are conducted by internal teams, while external audits are performed by third parties to provide an independent assessment.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

The virtualQ system offers two main optimizers: the Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO) and the Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO). 

The choice between optimizers depends on the optimization goal a customer wants to achieve and the data available. On a high level, the optimizers are classified by their optimization goals:

- Optimizers like FO, DO, and PO are focused on **peak management**.
- Optimizers like VQ and SO are focused on **waiting time calculation**.

Additionally, the system uses machine learning models in its core to predict the best times for offering callbacks, which supports the optimization process. The specific roles of AFO and APO are not detailed in the provided context, but they are part of this broader optimization framework within virtualQ.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

**Internal Audits:**
- Focus on six different pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability.
- Show where the implementation diverges from best practices.
- Carried out once or twice a year.
- Findings are tracked as technical debt and followed up according to their criticality.
- Involve participants such as the Chief Executive Officer, Head of Engineering, agents, and partners.
- Involve internal and external reviews, architecture, and design sessions in the team.

**External Audits:**
- Based on external tooling/services.
- Verify the virtualQ system either in the code base or the live system in a non-production stage.
- Further manual security-related audits (penetration testing) are carried out by a partner.

**Differences:**
- **Internal Audits** focus on evaluating internal processes, adherence to best practices, and overall operational efficiency and are often team-driven with internal reviews.
- **External Audits** involve third-party verification, often focusing on specific technical aspects such as code and system integrity, and include services from external partners.

The context does not provide a detailed comparison or contrast; hence, the distinctions are inferred from the descriptions provided.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

virtualQ offers the following optimizers, each with specific functions:

1. **Flexible Optimizer (FO)** - Used for peak management.
2. **Dynamic Optimizer (DO)** - Also used for peak management and requires data connection.
3. **Predictive Optimizer (PO)** - Used for peak management and requires data connection.
4. **virtualQ Algorithm (VQ)** - Used for waiting time calculation and requires data connection.
5. **Static Optimizer (SO)** - Used for peak management.

These optimizers/algorithms help in various optimization goals such as peak management or waiting time calculation, and their specific use depends on the optimization goal and available data.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
**Legal criteria for using 3rd‑party software (as defined in the context)**  

1. **Data‑protection compliance**  
   - The software must respect EU‑GDPR requirements, including any geo‑location restrictions on where the service and its data may reside.  
   - Data‑privacy agreements must be reviewed to ensure the 3rd‑party provider can be listed in the Data‑Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.

2. **Licensing & IP ownership**  
   - The component’s license must explicitly permit **commercial use** and allow virtualQ to **sell the complete product** that incorporates the software.  
   - Open‑source licences are examined to confirm they do not impose restrictions that would conflict with virtualQ’s commercial model.  
   - Ownership of any intellectual‑property rights must be clear, so virtualQ can safely integrate and distribute the software.

3. **Regulatory‑specific requirements**  
   - For customers subject to **GDPR**, the **German Social Code (SGB)**, or **critical‑infrastructure (KRITIS)** regulations, the software must meet the stricter security and compliance obligations defined by the Federal Office for IT Security (BSI).  
   - This includes the ability to apply security patches promptly.

4. **Operational/legal risk mitigation**  
   - The software must not create lock‑in or expose virtualQ to end‑of‑life (EoL) risks that could jeopardise continued operation or compliance.  
   - It should be possible for **maintenance to be performed by parties other than the original owner**, implying good documentation and supportability.

5. **Documentation & maintainability**  
   - The component should be well‑documented so that virtualQ (or another maintainer) can sustain it without relying solely on the original vendor.

These criteria together ensure that any 3rd‑party library or service can be used safely, legally, and commercially without exposing virtualQ to privacy breaches, licensing violations, or regulatory non‑compliance.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

**Internal audits**

* Performed inside the organisation.  
* Focus on **design verification** and overall compliance with the six audit pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability).  
* Carried out by internal participants – the **Head of Engineering**, engineering agents and internal partners.  
* Findings are recorded as technical debt and tracked for remediation according to their criticality.  
* Typically scheduled **once or twice a year**.

**External audits**

* Conducted by **third‑party tools or services** that are not part of the internal development team.  
* Verify the virtualQ system either **in the code base** or the **live system** (in a non‑production stage).  
* Include **manual security‑related audits such as penetration testing**, which are performed by an external partner.  
* The external audit also maps the same six pillars, but it provides an **independent assessment** of how the implementation aligns with best practices.  

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Internal audit | External audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Who performs it** | Internal staff (Head of Engineering, agents, internal partners) | External tooling/services and external security partners |
| **Scope of verification** | Design verification and internal compliance tracking | Code‑base and live‑system verification, plus independent security testing (penetration tests) |
| **Perspective** | In‑house view, focuses on tracking technical debt | Independent, third‑party view to confirm adherence to best practices |
| **Frequency** | Usually once or twice a year (same as external) | Same schedule, but executed by external resources |
| **Outcome handling** | Findings logged as technical debt and followed up by internal teams | Findings provide an external validation and may trigger additional remediation actions |

In short, internal audits are an **in‑house review** of design and compliance, while external audits are **independent checks** performed with third‑party tools and partners, especially for security verification. Both feed into the same audit cycle but differ in who conducts them and the level of independence they provide.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

**Optimizers that virtualQ provides**

| Optimizer | What it does (as described in the documentation) |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** | A flexible, rule‑based optimizer that can be applied to a variety of **peak‑management** goals. It is suited for situations where the optimisation goal is to control or smooth usage peaks (referred to in the text as “FO, DO, PO”). |
| **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** | An optimizer that relies on **training data** and AI/ML models to make predictions about future demand and then uses those predictions to drive the optimisation. It is especially useful for **waiting‑time calculations** and other predictive use‑cases (referred to as “VQ, SO”). |

**How the choice is made**

- The “best fit” optimizer depends on the **optimisation goal** a customer wants to achieve (e.g., peak management vs. waiting‑time reduction) and on the **data that is available** to the algorithms.  
- When the goal is peak management (FO, DO, PO), the **AFO** is typically selected.  
- When the goal is to predict demand or waiting times (VQ, SO), the **APO** is the appropriate choice because it can use historical training data to generate forecasts.

These are the two distinct optimizer families that virtualQ currently offers, each targeting a different class of optimisation problems.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

- Ensuring compliance with data privacy regulations, especially the EU’s GDPR, as well as requirements from customers regulated under social code (Sozialgesetzbuch, SGB) and those operating critical infrastructure (KRITIS).
- Carefully considering the geo-location of services and data privacy agreements, particularly for services provided by third-party providers, as they may need to be listed in Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
- Evaluating software licenses, especially when integrating open source components, to ensure they are compatible with commercial use. Not all open source licenses are permissible in a commercial context.
- Maintaining and regularly updating a list of approved licenses in consultation with legal experts.
- Monitoring IP ownership issues, particularly relevant in areas such as generative AI, to avoid potential legal risks.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits are evaluations focused on six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, and Sustainability. They assess where implementations diverge from best practices, are conducted once or twice a year, and their findings are tracked as technical debt and followed up based on criticality. Participants include the Head of Engineering.

External audits involve the use of external tooling or services to verify the virtualQ system, either in the code base or in a non-production stage of the live system. They also include manual security-related audits such as penetration testing carried out by a partner. Participants include the Chief Executive Officer, Head of Engineering, and an external security advisor.

The main differences are that internal audits are conducted internally and focus on broader operational and technical best practices, while external audits rely on external tools and partners to verify system security and code integrity. Additionally, external audits involve a wider range of participants, including external advisors and leadership, whereas internal audits primarily involve internal technical leadership.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

1. Ensuring compliance with EU’s GDPR regulations, especially concerning data privacy.
2. Considering geo-location of services and their data privacy agreements.
3. Evaluating licenses to ensure they allow virtualQ to use the component in a commercial way, including the ability to sell the whole product.

Internal and external audits are both practices used to verify the virtualQ system, but they have distinct differences.

**Internal Audits & Design Verification**:
- These audits focus on verifying the system's design and internal processes.
- They ensure that the system adheres to internal best practices and standards.
- The goal is to identify technical debt and areas for improvement within the organization.

**External Audits**:
- External audits involve external tooling/services that verify the virtualQ system.
- They can either examine the code base or the live system in a non-production stage.
- Manual security-related audits, such as penetration testing, are often carried out by a partner.
- These audits focus on six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
- Findings from external audits are tracked as technical debt and followed up according to their criticality.

**Differences**:
- **Scope**: Internal audits are more focused on internal processes and best practices, while external audits involve external verification tools/services.
- **Frequency**: Both internal and external audits are carried out once or twice a year, but the methods and focus can vary.
- **Participants**: Internal audits typically involve internal teams, while external audits may involve external partners, especially for security-related audits.
- **Focus**: Internal audits emphasize design verification and internal best practices, whereas external audits emphasize adherence to broader industry standards and external verification.

Please note that the context provided does not contain specific details on the exact processes or methodologies for both types of audits, but it outlines the general focus and purpose of each.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
**Legal criteria for using 3rd‑party software (as defined in the document)**  

1. **Compliance with data‑protection regulations**  
   * The software must respect EU‑GDPR requirements, including any geo‑location constraints on where the service and its data may reside.  
   * Data‑privacy agreements must be acceptable for virtualQ and its clients; services run by a 3rd‑party provider may need to be listed in the Data‑Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its customers.

2. **Licensing and IP ownership**  
   * The licence of the component must allow **commercial use** and **redistribution/sale of the whole product**.  
   * Open‑source licences are evaluated to ensure they do not impose restrictions that conflict with virtualQ’s commercial model.  

3. **Sector‑specific regulatory requirements**  
   * For customers subject to the German Social Code (SGB) or operating critical infrastructure (KRITIS), the software must meet the stricter obligations defined by those regimes, which go beyond the baseline set by the Federal Office of IT Security (BSI).

4. **Security obligations**  
   * The component must allow virtualQ to apply security patches promptly, satisfying the “apply patches as soon as possible” requirement mandated for regulated customers.

5. **Documentation and maintainability**  
   * Although not a pure legal point, the documentation is considered part of the legal risk assessment: the component should be well‑documented so that maintenance can be performed by parties other than the original owner, reducing reliance on a single vendor.

These criteria together ensure that any 3rd‑party library or service can be used without creating legal exposure, while still meeting the high‑privacy and security standards required by virtualQ’s regulated customers.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
**Internal audits**

* Performed by the organisation’s own staff (e.g., the Head of Engineering and the engineering team).  
* Conducted through internal reviews, design‑verification sessions and architecture workshops.  
* Focus on checking the implementation against the six audit pillars (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation, Sustainability) and identifying technical‑debt items that diverge from best practice.  
* Findings are tracked and followed‑up by the internal team according to their criticality.  

**External audits**

* Carried out by parties outside the organisation – either external tooling/services or a third‑party partner that performs manual security tests such as penetration testing.  
* The external tools verify the virtualQ system either in the code base or in a live, non‑production environment.  
* A partner‑run security audit (penetration testing) is also part of the external audit scope.  
* Results are reported back to the internal team and are treated as technical‑debt items in the same way, but the assessment is performed by an independent, external source.  

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Internal audit | External audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Who performs it** | Internal staff (Head of Engineering, engineering team) | External tooling/services and third‑party security partner |
| **Where it is applied** | Internal reviews, design‑verification sessions, architecture workshops | Code base or live system in a non‑production stage, plus manual penetration testing |
| **Purpose** | Verify compliance with internal best‑practice pillars and track technical debt | Provide an independent validation of the system’s security and overall compliance using outside expertise |
| **Frequency** | Conducted once or twice a year (same cadence as external audits) | Same cadence, but the execution is by external resources |

Thus, internal audits are the organisation’s own checks of design and implementation, while external audits are independent assessments using outside tools and partners to validate the system.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

response:
**Optimizers available in the virtualQ system**

| Optimizer | Primary purpose / optimisation goal | Typical data‑connection requirement |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| **Flexible Optimizer (FO)** | Used for **peak‑management** – helps the system allocate resources and schedule work so that demand spikes are handled efficiently. | No external data connection needed (stand‑alone). |
| **Dynamic Optimizer (DO)** | Also targets **peak‑management**, but adapts continuously to changing conditions (e.g., real‑time demand fluctuations). | Requires a data connection to receive up‑to‑date demand information. |
| **Predictive Optimizer (PO)** | A **peak‑management** tool that forecasts future demand and plans resource allocation accordingly. | Requires a data connection for feeding historical and real‑time data into the prediction model. |
| **virtualQ Algorithm (VQ)** | Designed for **waiting‑time calculation** – estimates how long callers will wait and can be used to balance load across queues. | Requires a data connection to obtain current queue‑state data. |
| **Static Optimizer (SO)** | Another **waiting‑time calculation** method that uses a fixed set of rules (does not change in real time). | No external data connection required. |
| **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)** | An automated version of the Flexible Optimizer; it performs the same peak‑management function but with less manual configuration. | Same requirements as FO (no data connection). |
| **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)** | An automated version of the Predictive Optimizer; it runs the forecasting‑based peak‑management logic automatically. | Same requirements as PO (needs a data connection). |

**In short**

- **Peak‑management optimizers** (FO, DO, PO, plus their automated counterparts AFO/APO) focus on handling demand spikes and allocating resources efficiently.
- **Waiting‑time optimizers** (VQ, SO) focus on estimating and managing how long callers wait in the queue.
- Some optimizers need a live data feed (DO, PO, VQ, APO) while others can operate without it (FO, SO, AFO).
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

- Ensuring compliance with data privacy regulations, especially the EU’s GDPR, as well as requirements from customers regulated under social code (Sozialgesetzbuch, SGB) and those operating critical infrastructure (KRITIS).
- Carefully considering the geo-location of services and data privacy agreements, particularly for services provided by third-party providers, as they may need to be listed in Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
- Evaluating software licenses, especially when integrating open source components, since not all open source licenses are suitable for commercial use. virtualQ maintains and regularly updates a list of approved licenses in consultation with legal experts.
- Monitoring intellectual property (IP) ownership, which is particularly important in the context of generative AI and the use of open source software.

Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
We use the following programming languages in the virtualQ system:

- **Ruby** (43% of the codebase) – used for application logic.
- **HTML / JavaScript** (24% of the codebase) – used for user interfaces.
- **Python** (11% of the codebase) – used for machine learning and AI.
- **.Net / C#** (9% of the codebase) – used for legacy ACD connectors (no longer sold, only maintained).
- **Elixir** (7% of the codebase) – used for application logic, seen as a functional evolution of Ruby.
- **Other** (6% of the codebase) – includes tools like Terraform Templates.

The codebase is being consolidated toward Ruby and Elixir for application logic, while HTML/JavaScript remain for user interfaces and Python for machine learning and AI.

response:
Internal audits involve reviews conducted within the organization, including architecture and design sessions within the team, as well as internal reviews to verify the system's design and implementation.

External audits are based on external tooling or services that verify the virtualQ system either in the code base or in a non-production stage of the live system. Additionally, manual security-related audits, such as penetration testing, are carried out by a partner.

The key difference is that internal audits are performed by the organization's own team and focus on design and development processes, while external audits use third-party tools or partners to assess the system's security and performance, often from an outsider's perspective.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

virtualQ offers two main optimizers: the Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO) and the Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO).

The Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO) is designed for the optimization goal of Peak Management. It uses predicted load in the contact center to manage incoming calls by converting them into callbacks, which helps in balancing the workload during peak times.

The context does not provide specific details about the functionality of the Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO), only its name and section reference. Therefore, no further description of AFO's function can be given based on the provided information.
expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

response:
The legal criteria for 3rd party software include:

1. **Data Privacy and Legal Compliance**: 
    - Carefully considering data privacy agreements, especially for services run by 3rd party service providers. These services might need to be listed in the Data Protection Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.
    - Ensuring compliance with regulations such as the EU’s GDPR, which is crucial given the regulated data our organization works with.
    
2. **Licenses and Intellectual Property (IP) Ownership**:
    - Evaluating licenses to ensure that they allow virtualQ to use the components in a commercial way, including the ability to sell the whole product.
    - Ensuring that licenses permit the use of open-source components in integrating them into the virtualQ system.
    
3. **Maintenance and Documentation**:
    - Ensuring that the component is well documented and that maintenance can be done by someone other than the owner.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
Internal audits and external audits differ in their sources and focus. Here's a summary based on the provided context:

**Internal Audits:**
- Conducted internally by the team.
- Focuses on six different pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
- Aims to show where the implementation diverges from best practices.
- Carried out once or twice a year.
- Findings are tracked as technical debt and followed up based on their criticality.
- Participants include the Head of Engineering, agents, and partners.

**External Audits:**
- Based on external tooling/services that verify the virtualQ system either in the codebase or the live system in a non-production stage.
- Manual security-related audits (penetration testing) are carried out by a partner.
- External users without domain knowledge need interfaces to be intuitive and efficient.

In summary, internal audits are performed by the internal team to assess compliance with best practices across multiple dimensions, while external audits rely on external tools and services to verify the system's integrity and security.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.

1. **Automated Flexible Optimizer (AFO)**
2. **Automated Predictive Optimizer (APO)**

These optimizers are classified by their optimization goals and data connection requirements. Their specific functionalities and how they use data are described in the context:

- **Dynamic Optimizer**: This optimizer requires real-time data such as the number of agents online, idle agents, average handling time, and incoming calls over the past hour. It uses this data to calculate the current load in the contact center and does not apply ML/AI for its calculations.
  
- **Optimizers Based on Optimization Goals**: These include optimization goals such as peak management (FO, DO, PO) and waiting time calculation (VQ, SO). The specific optimizers (AFO and APO) likely serve these goals but the context does not provide detailed descriptions of each optimizer's specific function in relation to these goals.

expected_answer: VirtualQ provides a range of optimizers which are algorithms used to calculate caller waiting times in its intelligent callback system. Each optimizer fits different levels of data availability and customer goals. The Flexible Optimizer adapts to partial real time data while the Dynamic Optimizer relies on live ACD data to adjust callbacks instantly. The Predictive Optimizer uses machine learning with historical and real time inputs to forecast wait times and schedule callbacks proactively. The proprietary virtualQ Algorithm offers a general solution when deeper integrations are not possible and the Static Optimizer uses fixed rules for environments with little or no real time data. Automated variants such as the Automated Flexible Optimizer and Automated Predictive Optimizer further reduce manual setup and improve adaptation over time. Together these options let virtualQ support customers across a wide range of integration depths and data richness.

**Legal criteria for using 3rd‑party software (as defined by virtualQ):**

- **GDPR compliance** – the software must handle personal data in a way that satisfies the EU General Data Protection Regulation.  
- **Geo‑location & data‑privacy agreements** – the location of the service and its privacy terms must be reviewed to ensure they meet virtualQ’s data‑privacy requirements.  
- **DPA listing** – any 3rd‑party service that processes virtualQ data may need to be listed in the Data‑Processing Agreements (DPAs) that virtualQ shares with its clients.  
- **License suitability** – the component’s license must allow:
  - Commercial use of the software,  
  - Inclusion in a product that can be sold to customers, and  
  - Redistribution of the whole product.  
- **IP ownership checks** – verify that the intellectual‑property rights attached to the component do not create conflicts, especially for open‑source and generative‑AI‑related code.  
- **Approved‑license list** – the component must be on virtualQ’s maintained list of licenses that have been vetted by legal counsel; this list is continuously updated.  
- **Maintenance & documentation** – the component should be well documented and maintainable by someone other than the original owner.  
- **Security‑patch readiness** – ensure that security updates can be applied promptly after they are released.  

These criteria are evaluated before any external library or tool is adopted to avoid legal issues, lock‑in, or end‑of‑life problems.
expected_answer: virtualQ evaluates third-party software based on strict legal and compliance requirements focused on GDPR-aligned data privacy license compatibility IP protection and regulatory adherence. Software must ensure clear data locality secure handling and proper inclusion in DPAs. All licenses—especially open source—must allow unrestricted commercial use and not threaten virtualQ’s IP rights. Tools are checked for long-term support security (via audits Snyk) and must avoid outdated or risky components. Preference is given to portable industry-standard technologies to prevent vendor lock-in.

response:
**Internal audits**

* Performed by the organisation’s own people (e.g., Head of Engineering, internal review teams).  
* Focus on **design verification** and **internal reviews** of the virtualQ system.  
* Examine the implementation against the six audit pillars – Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimisation and Sustainability.  
* Findings are recorded as technical‑debt items and are tracked and acted on according to their criticality.  
* Usually scheduled **once or twice a year** as part of the regular internal governance process.

**External audits**

* Conducted by **outside parties** using external tooling/services or a partner that performs manual security testing (penetration testing).  
* Verify the virtualQ system either **in the code base** or the **live system in a non‑production stage**.  
* Provide an independent, third‑party assessment of how the system aligns with best‑practice standards.  
* Results are also fed back into the audit process but are distinguished from internal reviews because they come from outside the organisation.

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Internal audit | External audit |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Who performs it** | Internal staff (Head of Engineering, internal review teams) | External tooling/services and external partners (e.g., penetration‑testing provider) |
| **Scope/Method** | Design verification, internal reviews, architecture sessions | Code‑base or live‑system checks in a non‑production environment; manual security testing |
| **Purpose** | Track technical debt, ensure compliance with internal standards and the six pillars | Obtain an independent validation of security and overall compliance, identify gaps that internal teams may miss |
| **Frequency** | Typically once or twice a year as part of the regular audit cycle | Conducted as part of the same audit cycle but relies on third‑party scheduling; may be less frequent or triggered by specific needs |

In summary, internal audits are **self‑conducted assessments** aimed at continuous improvement and debt tracking, while external audits are **independent evaluations** performed by outside tools or partners to verify the system’s security and compliance from an outsider’s perspective.
expected_answer: Internal audits focus on code quality design verification and vulnerability detection using automated tools like Debricked and Snyk mainly in non-production environments. They are part of ongoing development processes. External audits performed by independent partners include penetration tests that simulate real attacks to validate the security of customer-facing systems. In essence internal audits proactively maintain code and process integrity while external audits provide independent assurance of virtualQ’s overall security posture.
